## Khuddakanikāya
## Nettippakaraṇa-Aṭṭhakathā
## Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
## Ganthārambhakathā

I pay homage to the Lord, the Refuge, who is endowed with great compassion, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of knowable things, and who taught the Dhamma with subtle, profound, and diverse methods.

I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, well-honored by the Fully Enlightened One, by means of which those endowed with knowledge and conduct escape from the world.

I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the incomparable field of merit, who are endowed with virtues such as morality and are established in the paths and fruits.

By the power of the merit generated by thus paying homage to the Triple Gem, may all obstacles be destroyed in every place. Having been respectfully requested by the Elder named Dhammarakkhita, who desires the long endurance of the Nettippakaraṇa, the guide to the True Dhamma;

The Elder Mahākaccāyana, who saw the fulfillment of the aspiration he made at the feet of the Lord Padumuttara; who was placed in the foremost rank by the Buddha, who declared, "He is the foremost among those who explain in detail what has been spoken in brief"; who is the most excellent among the great disciples, endowed with the six higher powers, having attained mastery, possessing the analytical insights, and praised by the Fully Enlightened One...
2:
There exists that Netti text, spoken by the Elder Mahākaccāyana, approved by the Teacher (the Buddha), which is always connected with the nine-fold Dispensation (Sāsana) and serves as an explanation of its meaning.

Although it is difficult for me to compose a commentary (aṭṭhakathā) on this Netti text because it must be delved into by those of deep wisdom, I shall nevertheless compose an explanation of its meaning according to my ability. I do so because the Dispensation of the Teacher, together with its commentaries, endures, and the decisions of the former great teachers remain. Therefore, relying on those decisions, delving into the five Nikāyas, and comparing it with the Peṭakopadesa, I will compose a commentary that is very pure, unmixed, and contains subtle analytical decisions, without contradicting the traditions of the dwellers of the Mahāvihāra.

Avoiding errors made through negligence, aligning well with the Pali text, and clarifying the methods (upadesa), I shall compose the commentary. Thus, O virtuous ones, listen respectfully as I analyze the unmixed meaning of the Nettippakaraṇa.

In that context, for what reason is it called "Netti"? It is called Netti in the sense of leading (nayana) to the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). Just as craving is called "bhavanetti" because it leads beings to existence such as the sensual realm, so too this text is called "Netti" because it leads beings who are to be guided (venayeya) to the Noble Dhamma. Alternatively, it is called Netti because one is led by it. Indeed, by means of this Nettippakaraṇa as an instrument, Dhamma preachers lead beings to the Path of Vision (dassanamagga). Or, it is called Netti because beings are established in this text as a foundation and are led to Nibbāna. Indeed, without relying on the methods of the Netti, it is impossible to have an unerring understanding of the meaning of the Suttas. Thus it was said (in the Peṭakopadesa): "Therefore, one desiring to attain Nibbāna..." and so forth. All commentaries on the meaning of the Suttas depend on the Netti methods; the Netti originates from the Suttas, and the Suttas originate from the Fully Enlightened One.

Furthermore, this Netti is threefold by way of the divisions of the text: Hāra (Modes of Conveyance), Naya (Methods), and Paṭṭhāna (Pattern of the Dispensation). First is the investigation of Hāra, then the investigation of Naya, and finally the investigation of Paṭṭhāna. By way of the arrangement of the Pali, it is twofold: Saṅgahavāra (Summary Section) and Vibhāgavāra (Explanation Section). Indeed, the entire Netti consists only of these two sections: Saṅgahavāra and Vibhāgavāra.
3:
In that text, the Saṅgahavāra is defined at the beginning by five verses. There is no meaning of the text that is not encompassed by these five verses beginning with "Yaṃ loko pūjayate". Here, one might ask: "Is it not true that the Paṭṭhāna (Sāsanapaṭṭhāna) is not included in these five verses?" It should not be viewed in this way, because the Paṭṭhāna is indeed included by the inclusion of the "Root Terms" (Mūlapada). For it will be said later: "The eighteen root terms are to be seen in the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna." Indeed, the Mūlapada and the Paṭṭhāna are mutually inclusive, just like the three-fold meaning-methods and the triad of formations (saṅkhāra-tika).

The Vibhāgavāra is threefold by way of Uddesa (Brief Statement), Niddesa (Exposition), and Paṭiniddesa (Detailed Exposition). Among these, from "Tattha katame soḷasa hārā" until "bhavanti aဋ္ဌārasa padāni" is the Uddesavāra. From "Assādādīnavatā" until "tettiṃsā ettikā nettī" is the Niddesavāra. The Paṭiniddesavāra is fourfold: Hāravibhaṅgavāra, Hārasampātavāra, Nayasamuṭṭhānavāra, and Sāsanapaṭṭhānavāra. Among these, from "Tattha katamo desanāhāro" until "ayaṃ pahānena samāropanā" is the Hāravibhaṅgavāra. Therein, from "Katamo desanāဟာရsampāto" until "anupādisesā ca nibbānadhātū" is the Hārasampātavāra.

Here it is asked: "What is the difference between Hāravibhaṅgavāra and Hārasampātavāra?" It is said: Where a single Hāra is explained through many example Suttas, that is Hāravibhaṅgavāra. But where many Hāras converge in a single Sutta, that is Hārasampātavāra. This meaning was stated in the Peṭaka: "Where all Hāras, converging because of the variety of grammatical methods, lead to the meaning of the Sutta, that ground is Hārasampātavāra."

The distinction between Nayasamuṭṭhānavāra and Sāsanapaṭṭhānavāra is quite clear. However, Sāsanapaṭṭhānavāra is not explicitly extracted in the Uddesa and Niddesa sections as it is in the Saṅgahavāra. Here it is asked: "How is it known that this Nettippakaraṇa was spoken by a Great Disciple and approved by the Blessed One?" It is known through the Pali itself. There is no authority higher than the Pali. That Pali which does not contradict the four Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa) is the standard. Likewise, this Nettippakaraṇa has been brought down by an irreproachable lineage of teachers, just like the Peṭakopadesa. If that is so, why is its prologue (nidāna) not stated? For even in Suttas spoken by disciples, such as the Subha Sutta and Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, the prologue is stated, is it not?
4:
If it is asked whether the prologue (nidāna) of the Kaccāyana-saṃyutta and so forth was spoken, this statement regarding the presence or absence of a prologue is not absolute. For, in some disciple-spoken texts such as the Paṭisambhidāmagga and Mahāniddesa, as well as in some Buddha-spoken texts such as the Dhammapada and Buddhavaṃsa, no prologue is spoken. Just because a prologue is not mentioned, it cannot be said that those texts are not authoritative; the same should be understood here in this Netti text.

In fact, what is called the prologue of the Suttas and Vinaya was spoken only by Great Disciples such as the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, and the Venerable Upāli. This Netti text was also spoken by a Great Disciple (the Venerable Mahākaccāyana). Since this is not the domain of anyone other than the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, what is the use of searching for a prologue? Only the meaning that is not contrary to the Pāḷi should be sought in this text. Alternatively, since it is a commentary (aṭṭhakathā) explaining the meaning of the Pāḷi, it should be understood that there is no need for a separate prologue in this text, just as in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, Mahāniddesa, and so forth.

Now, in order to provide skill in various aspects of this text, this classification should be understood: This entire text is of one kind (ekavidha) by way of seeking the meaning of the Dispensation (sāsanapariyeṭṭhi), as well as by way of accomplishing the Noble Path and by way of the taste of liberation.

It is of two kinds (duvidha) by way of the composition of phrasing and meaning; by way of the Summary Section (saṅgahavāra) and the Classification Section (vibhāgavāra); by way of explaining the meaning of the Dhamma and Vinaya; by way of encompassing mundane and supramundane meanings; by way of grasping material and immaterial phenomena; by way of the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) and the characterized (lakkhiya); by way of speaking of arising (vaṭṭa) and cessation (nibbāna); by way of describing similar (sabhāga) and dissimilar (visabhāga) states; and by way of classifying common (sādhāraṇa) and uncommon (asādhāraṇa) states.

It is of three kinds (tividha) by way of describing three types of persons; by way of classifying the three types of excellence (kalyāṇa); by way of speaking of the three types of full understanding (pariññā); by way of pointing out the three types of abandonment (pahāna); by way of encompassing the three trainings (sikkhā); by way of purifying the three types of defilement (saṃkilesa); by way of the distinctions of the original song (mūlagīti), the follow-up song (anugīti), and the rehearsal (saṅgīti); by way of explaining the meaning of the three Piṭakas; and by way of the distinctions of the modes (hāra), the methods (naya), and the foundations (paṭṭhāna).

It is of four kinds (catubbidha) by way of being the domain of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); by way of teaching through the four methods; and by way of the profundity of the Dhamma, the meaning (attha), the teaching (desanā), and the penetration (paṭivedha). It is of five kinds (pañcavidha) by way of classifying states such as those to be fully known (abhiññeyya); by way of describing the five aggregates; by way of defining the five destinations (gati); and by way of explaining the meaning of the five Nikāyas. It is of six kinds (chabbidha) by way of classifying the six objects and by way of classifying the six internal and external sense bases. It is of seven kinds (sattavidha) by way of defining the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). It is of nine kinds (navavidha) by way of describing the nine limbs (aṅga) such as the Suttas. It is of fourteen kinds (cuddasavidha) by way of classifying the foundations of the Suttas. It is of sixteen kinds (soḷasavidha) and twenty-eight kinds (aṭṭhavīsatividha) by way of the distinctions of the foundations of the Dispensation (sāsanapaṭṭhāna). It is of eighty-four thousand kinds (caturāsītisahassavidha) by way of investigating the eighty-four thousand groups of Dhamma. In this manner, the classification of the text should be understood.

Among those classifications, "by way of seeking the meaning of the Dispensation" (sāsanapariyeṭṭhi) means that the entire Netti text is a commentary explaining the meaning of the Teacher's Dispensation, which encompasses the three trainings and consists of nine limbs.
5:
"By accomplishing the Noble Path" (ariyāmaggasampādanato) means by accomplishing the stage of seeing and the stage of development. "By the taste of liberation" (vimuttirasato) is said because the Dispensation has the Deathless Nibbāna as its end. "By way of the investigation of phrasing and meaning" (byañjanatthavicārabhāvato) is said because the modes (hāra), the phrasing (byañjanapada), and the action-methods (kammanaya) investigate the phrasing, while the meaning-phrasing (atthapada) and the meaning-methods (atthanaya) investigate the meaning. The nature of the Summary Section and the Classification Section will become clear later. "By way of explaining the meaning of the Dhamma and Vinaya" (dhammavinayatthasaṃvaṇṇanato) is said because the entire scriptural Dispensation (pariyatti-sāsana) consists of Dhamma and Vinaya. "By way of the characteristic and the characterized" (lakkhaṇalakkhiyabhāvato) is said because the Netti text is the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) and the example suttas are the characterized (lakkhiya). "By way of describing similar and dissimilar states" (sabhāgavisabhāganiddesato) means that states of a similar nature are called similar (sabhāga), and states that are opposites are called dissimilar (visabhāga); it refers to the investigation of these states. "By way of classifying common and uncommon states" (sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇadhammavibhāgato) means that states which are associated by way of commonality, such as having a single purpose in abandonment or a single purpose in co-existence, and are common in name and substance, are called common (sādhāraṇa); those that are the opposite of such common states are uncommon (asādhāraṇa). It is of two kinds by way of classifying these common and uncommon states.

"By way of describing three types of persons" (puggalattayaniddesato) means by way of describing the three types of persons such as the one of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū). "By way of classifying the three types of excellence" (tividhakalyāṇavibhāgato) means by way of classifying the excellence in the beginning (ādikalyāṇa) and so forth. "By way of the distinctions of the original song, the follow-up song, and the rehearsal" (mūlagīti-anugīti-saṅgītibhedato) means that the first speech is called the original song (mūlagīti); the verse that summarizes the meaning already spoken is called the follow-up song (anugīti); the harmonious recital of the text, which was scattered by way of connecting the meanings of various suttas, is called the rehearsal (saṅgīti). It should be understood that this rehearsal was performed later by the Elder (Mahākaccāyana). It is of three kinds by way of the distinctions of these three: original song, follow-up song, and rehearsal. "By way of describing the five aggregates" (pañcakkhandhaniddesato) means it is of five kinds by way of describing the five aggregates such as the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha) and the five Dhamma-aggregates such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). "By way of classifying the foundations of the Suttas" (suttādhiṭṭhānavibhāgato) means it is of fourteen kinds by way of classifying the fourteen foundations of the Suttas through the power of greed, hate, delusion, non-greed, non-hate, non-delusion, bodily action, verbal action, mental action, and the five faculties such as faith. The remaining points are not elaborated upon as they are easy to understand.

## 1. Description of the Summary Section (Saṅgahavāra-vaṇṇanā)

In this Netti text, which is classified in many ways as described above, it was said: "It is of two kinds by way of the Summary Section and the Classification Section." Therein, the Summary Section (saṅgahavāra) is the beginning. In that Summary Section, this verse beginning with "Yaṃ loko pūjayate" is the beginning. In that verse, the word "Yaṃ" (Which) is a designation of the object (kamma) in an indefinite sense; its definite identification should be understood by the word "tassa" (to him). "Loko" (the world) is the designation of the agent (kattā). "Pūjayate" (honors) is the designation of the verb (kiriyā). "Salokapālo" (together with the world-protectors) is the qualifier of the agent. "Sadā" (always) is the designation of time. "Namassati ca" (and pays homage) includes the word "ca" which has the sense of aggregation...
6:
It is an indication of the verb. "Tassa" is an indication by the genitive case (possession). "Etaṃ" is an indication by the nominative case (subject). "Sāsanavaraṃ" is the demonstration of the Dhamma indicated by the nominative case. "Vidūhi" is an indication of the agent by the instrumental case. "Ñeyyaṃ" is an indication of the passive verb. "Naravarassa" is the demonstration of the specific meaning designated by the term "tassa."

In that verse, regarding the word "lokiyaṃ," it means the world, beings, or the assembly of beings, because wholesome and unwholesome actions and their results (vipāka) exist in this assembly of beings. The word "loka" is a generic term (jātishadda) and thus encompasses all beings without exception. Although the word "loka" is also seen used for the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) and the world of locations (okāsaloka/bhājana), it should be understood that here it refers only to the world of beings (sattaloka) because of their worthiness to be worshipped. "Pūjayate" means to cherish or to pay respect.

They are called "lokapāla" because they protect the world; these are the Four Great Kings. Secular teachers, however, say that the gods Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kuvera are the world-guardians. It is called "salokapāla" because it exists together with the world-guardians; it is in apposition (tulyādhikaraṇa) with the word "loka." Alternatively, the Kings, the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Paranimmitavasavatti, Mahābrahmā, and so on, are called world-guardians because they protect and guard the respective worlds of beings through their sovereignty and authority. The assembly of various beings together with them is called "the world with its world-guardians" (salokapālo loko). Alternatively, according to the saying, "Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world," moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa) are called world-guardians. The world endowed with these qualities is called "salokapāla." For the virtuous who are endowed with hiri and ottappa and who loathe evil, being desirous of the Dhamma, are devoted to worshipping and paying homage to the Blessed One.

"Sadā" means at all times, both night and day. Or, "sadā" refers to the period while the Blessed One was alive and the period thereafter. Alternatively, "sadā" means from the time of the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) until the disappearance of the Dispensation, or even beyond that. For from the time of the great aspiration, the Great Bodhisattas, being certain of enlightenment and thus being "Buddha-sprouts" (buddhaṅkura), are worthy of worship and homage by the world including the devas. As the Blessed One said when he was the hermit Sumedha:

"Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings, having praised my deed, raised his right foot."
7:
"Those sons of the Conqueror who were present there circumambulated me. Devas, humans, and asuras, having paid homage, departed." (Buddhavamsa).

Regarding the phrase "and pays homage" (namassati ca): some people perform offerings and hospitality to others but do not pay homage because the virtues of those recipients are not evident. It is not so with the Blessed One; because His fame has spread according to His actual virtues, the world with its devas both honors and pays homage to the Blessed One. Some read "sadā naramanusso," but that reading is not good. "Tassa" means: of that Noble Man (the Buddha) whom the world with its devas honors and pays homage to. By the word "etaṃ," the meaning that is currently revolving in one's own intellect is indicated in a general way. By the word "sāsanavaraṃ," that same meaning is indicated in its specific form.

In that term "sāsanavaraṃ": it is called "sāsana" (dispensation/instruction) because by this Dhamma, beings are instructed and disciplined according to their fitness for the benefits of the present life, the benefits of the future life, and the ultimate benefit (paramattha). That very dispensation is called "vara" (noble/excellent) in the sense of being noble because it definitely leads out of the round of suffering (niyyānika) and because it possesses unique virtues. Or, it is called "vara" because it is desired by the wise as it is the cause for the fulfillment of various desired prosperities. Since the dispensation itself is noble, it is called "sāsanavaraṃ" (the noble dispensation). "Vidūhi" refers to the wise who know things as they really are, such as kamma and its results, and the various dhammas like the wholesome and so on. It is called "ñeyyaṃ" because it is to be known by those wise ones, or because it is worthy of being known. "Naravarassa" means of the Noble Man, the Supreme Person.

This is the intended meaning: The Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is worthy of honor and homage by the world with its devas due to His possession of unique qualities such as Great Compassion and Omniscience—this dispensation of that Supreme Person in the world is now the object of our investigation into the Hāra, Naya, and Paṭṭhāna to be analyzed; it is noble, supreme, and excellent because it is endowed with qualities such as being good in the beginning; and because it is the domain of subtle knowledge, it is to be known only by the wise. For the word of the Blessed One, even if it is only a single verse, is extremely profound because it is capable of extracting the nature of truths (sacca), dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), faculties (indriya), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and so on, and because it is suitable for investigation through the sixteen Hāra, the five Naya, and the sixteen or twenty-eight types of Paṭṭhāna. In terms of meaning, it is like a shoreless ocean, the domain of only subtle and fine knowledge. Therefore, He said: "This Dhamma is for the wise, not for the unwise." Alternatively, the Blessed One's dispensation is to be entered through the sequence of full understanding (pariññā), through the practice of realizing characteristics, and through the doors of emptiness (suññatamukha), etc.; thus, it is not the domain of the ignorant even in their dreams. Therefore, He said: "to be known by the wise." Accordingly, it was said: "Let a wise man come," and so forth.
8:
Other teachers, however, read it as 'Taṃ tassa sāsanavaraṃ'. According to their view, the word 'yaṃ' should be understood as being in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) with the word 'sāsana'. The meaning is: the world together with its guardians honors and pays homage to that excellent Dispensation; that excellent Dispensation should be known by the wise. In this method, the word 'lokapāla' (world-guardian) also refers to the Blessed One. Because the Blessed One is the supreme guide (leader) of the world, he is literally called 'lokapāla'. Therefore, 'tassa' means 'of the Teacher who is the world-guardian'. In this term 'salokapālo', although the word 'lokapāla' is subordinate (guṇībhūta), because it pertains to the Buddha, because it regards the Dispensation, and because it is a qualifying term connected by way of lordship, it deserves to be referred back to (paṭiniddesa) by the word 'tassa' as if it were primary.

How does the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma (Dhammassāmī), honor the Dhamma? This is not contradictory. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, hold the Dhamma in high esteem; they always dwell respecting the Dhamma. It has been said: 'What if I were to dwell honoring, respecting, and relying on this very Dhamma which I have fully awakened to?' (SN 1.173; AN 4.21). Furthermore, the Blessed One's honoring of the Dhamma is shown through practices such as the seven weeks [after enlightenment]. The term 'Dhammassāmī' also means the lord of the world with its devas by means of the Dhamma, not the lord of the Dhamma. Even so, it might be said that the word 'homage' (namassati) is inappropriate, because the Blessed One does not pay homage to anyone. However, this is also faultless. For the word 'namassati' does not only mean performing an act of homage, but also carries the meaning of being inclined, leaned, and bent towards that Dhamma through holding it in high esteem. The Blessed One, because of his esteem for the Dhamma, always dwells in a state of being inclined, leaned, and bent towards the Dhamma. This meaning is shown by such Sutta passages as: 'I always dwell in this manner'. There is also the reading 'vidūhi neyyaṃ'; its meaning is that it should be led to (made known) in one's own continuity and the continuity of others by the wise. Therein, leading to one's own continuity means understanding it oneself, and leading to the continuity of others means making others understand it.

Thus, by stating his state of being worthy of honor and homage by the world with its devas and his state as the supreme person, the excellence of the Blessed One's qualities is shown. That excellence of qualities should be known through the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi). Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) which has the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints which has omniscience as its proximate cause, are called 'Mahābodhi'. That Mahābodhi is known to be well-established in the Tathāgata because of his teaching of the unerring Dhamma.
9:
It is understood. Indeed, such a teaching of the Dhamma is not possible without the abandonment of defilements along with their residual traces (vāsanā) and without unimpeded knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa). In this way, it shows the Blessed One's possession of the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa). Through that possession of intrepidity, the fulfillment of all the qualities of omniscience—such as the ten powers (bala), the six unshared knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), and the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadhamma)—is made manifest. Since such fulfillment of excellence cannot be obtained without the accumulation (sambhāra) of merit and wisdom—namely, the thirty perfections (pāramī) accomplished by placing great compassion at the forefront and the fulfillment of the aspiration for Buddhahood first—the fulfillment of the cause (hetu-sampadā) is also clarified by implication. Thus, it should be understood that by this verse, the Buddha's qualities in their entirety—which are the cause for all beings to obtain absolute welfare in all three stages and which are good in the beginning, middle, and end—are proclaimed.

In the second method, however, the world with its devas is said to honor [the Dispensation] because it practices with respect through hearing, retaining, and inquiring, etc., while reflecting on the possession of special qualities such as being well-expounded (svākkhāta), and while penetrating the truths as appropriate—namely, the Dispensation of the Noble Path which includes the three trainings along with its fruits, the deathless element of Nibbāna which is the object of that Path, the Dispensation of preliminary practice which is the means for attaining that Path and Nibbāna, and the Dispensation of scriptural study (pariyatti) which explains that meaning. The Blessed One, the Protector of the World, having attained perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), also honors [the Dhamma] by respectfully teaching the Dhamma to those to be led (veneyya), and by praising it with such words as: 'Monks, I will teach you the noble right concentration,' 'Of paths, the eightfold path is the best,' 'Monks, as far as there are dhammas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is said to be the foremost among them,' 'The destruction [of craving], dispassion, the deathless, the sublime,' 'Monks, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings,' and 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning,' and so forth. Therefore, by stating the worthiness of honor of the excellent Dispensation here, the qualities of the Dhamma are proclaimed without remainder. Thus, the many qualities of the Dhamma proclaimed in various Sutta passages—such as being noble (ariya), being leading out (niyyāna), the destruction and fading away of defilements, the crushing of pride (madanimmadana), being unconditioned (asaṅkhata), being well-expounded (svākkhāta), and being good in the beginning—should be understood as being proclaimed in their entirety by this verse.
10:
Because only those whose delusion has been completely eradicated through the penetration of the Noble Truths are, in the ultimate sense, called wise (paṇḍita). This is because they have transcended foolishness and the like. Therefore, the Noble Persons (ariya-puggala) who have developed the supramundane path and realized the fruits of recluseship are specifically called 'the wise' (vidū). Indeed, they are able to know the aforementioned sublime Teaching without distortion and to establish it in their own and others' continuums. Thus, because the ultimate Saṅgha, consisting of the group of eight Noble Persons, is included here, it should be understood that the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha, which are praised in various Sutta passages as 'practicing well' (suppaṭipannatā) and so on, are fully revealed here.

Having thus illustrated the supreme qualities of the Triple Gem with the first verse, now—

## Not doing any evil, the undertaking of what is skillful,
## The purification of one's own mind—this is the Teaching of the Buddhas.

According to these words, the Teaching, which briefly encompasses the Three Trainings, is of three types according to the distinction of the objects of specific knowledge and the distinction of stages. How? The Teaching called 'the True Dhamma of Scriptural Study' (pariyatti-saddhamma), which is the object of wisdom resulting from hearing (sutamaya-ñāṇa). The Teaching called 'the True Dhamma of Practice' (paṭipatti-saddhamma), which is the object of wisdom resulting from reflection (cintāmaya-ñāṇa), characterized by what is to be grasped through reflection on methods, investigation of views, and acceptance of ideas, and which is a specific cause for the fruit of Arahantship. The Teaching called 'the True Dhamma of Penetration' (paṭivedha-saddhamma), which is the object of wisdom resulting from mental development (bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa) occurring together with insight knowledge and so on. Having included these three types of Teaching under the term 'sublime Teaching' (sāsana-vara), and because the first among them, the Teaching of Scriptural Study, is the means for attaining the others, and is the root-basis of the entire Teaching as well as the scope of this very treatise, the author, wishing to first analyze the Teaching of Scriptural Study in brief, spoke the verse beginning with 'Twelve terms' (dvādasa padāni).

In that verse, 'twelve' (dvādasa) is the delimitation of number. 'Terms' (padāni) is the indication of the delimited dhammas. Among those terms, phrasing-terms (byañjana-pada) are called 'terms' (pada) because the meaning is reached (pajjati) through these phrasings. Meaning-terms (attha-pada), however, are called 'terms' because they are reached or known. Or rather, both should be applied in both ways, because phrasing-terms must be reached without distortion, and meaning-terms are the cause for the attainment of higher distinctions. Since those terms will be made clear later in the Pali text itself, I shall explain them right there. It is called 'Sutta' because of its meanings such as indicating the sense (attha-sūcana) and so on. Thus it is said in the commentaries—

## Because it indicates the meanings, is well-spoken, produces, and flows,
## Because it protects and is like a thread, it is called 'Sutta'.
11:
Although that statement (beginning with 'Because it indicates the meanings') occurs in those commentaries in the context of the Sutta Piṭaka, here in this Netti treatise, it should be applied in the context of the three Piṭakas. It is said, 'Twelve terms are the Sutta,' which means the Teaching of Scriptural Study (pariyatti-sāsana). 'All that' refers to the entire Buddha-word called 'Sutta'. It is because of the six phrasing-terms and the six meaning-terms, which are the meanings of those phrasings, that it is said, 'Twelve terms are the Sutta'.

The Dhamma of Scriptural Study is called 'Sutta' because of its meanings such as indicating the sense and so on. All that Sutta, in terms of its essence, consists of twelve terms: six phrasing-terms and six meaning-terms. Alternatively, all that Buddha-word called 'sublime Teaching' is called 'Sutta' because the Teaching of Scriptural Study is intended. In terms of meaning, however, it consists of twelve terms because it is a collection of phrasing-terms and meaning-terms. Therefore, the Venerable Kaccāna said, 'Phrasing and meaning' (byañjanañca attho ca). When phrasing and meaning are connected in the relationship of the expression and the expressed (vacana-vacanīya), the designation 'Sutta' arises; both of these should be known in their true nature. To make known which is phrasing and which is meaning among those two, he said, 'What is the meaning? Which is the phrasing?'

Having thus shown the nature of the Sutta called 'sublime Teaching' as Scriptural Study, and that it should be understood as phrasing-terms and meaning-terms, now, in order to show the Netti treatise, which is the means for investigating that Sutta, by way of the analysis of terms and meanings, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Sixteen modes' (soḷasa hārā).

In that verse, it is called 'Sixteen Modes' (soḷasa-hārā) because there are sixteen modes in this Netti treatise. The same method should be understood for the phrase 'five methods, eighteen root-terms'. Alternatively, the sixteen modes themselves are called 'Sixteen Modes'. The same applies to the other terms. Indeed, the modes, methods, and root-terms, spoken in brief and in detail, are called 'Netti'. 'Investigation of the Teaching' (sāsanassa pariyeṭṭhi) means searching for the meaning of the Teaching, or the explanation of the meaning of the Teaching of Scriptural Study. Or it can mean the investigation of the meaning of the entire Teaching. For even the Teaching of Practice and Penetration are attained by following the methods of the Netti. In the name 'Mahākaccāna', 'Kaccāna' is an ancient sage. This Great Elder, who is an ornament to that lineage, is called 'Kaccāna'. 'Mahākaccāna' is a title of respect, just like 'Mahāmoggallāna'. There is also a reading 'Kaccāyanagottaniddiṭṭhā'. It should be understood that this verse was placed by the teachers who redacted the Netti by way of summarizing the meaning of the treatise. It is just like the words 'Therefore the Venerable One said' at the conclusion of the descriptions of the various modes in the Hāravibhaṅgavāra. In the investigation of what is investigated by what in the Netti treatise, which is a collection of modes and so on, and in the Sutta, which is a collection of phrasing and meaning, he said, 'The modes are the investigation of phrasing,' and so on.
12: In that [passage regarding hāras and byañjanavicaya], the sixteen hāras, excluding the extraction of root terms (mūlapada), are commentaries on the sutta through the door of phrasing (byañjana) alone. They are not commentaries on the sutta through the door of extracting the nature of things (sabhāvadhammā) known as root terms, as the methods (naya) are. Therefore, those hāras are called 'the investigation of phrasing (byañjanavicaya) of the sutta.' The meaning-methods (atthanaya), however, lead to the realization of the meaning of the sutta through the door of the aforementioned meaning alone. Therefore, He said: 'The three methods are the meaning of the sutta.' This investigation will also appear later. Some teachers read 'Nayo ca,' but that reading is not good. 'Both are included' refers to the hāras and the nayas. Both are grasped comprehensively by way of extracting the meaning of the sutta and are applied to the sutta in every way. It explains the sutta. How? It explains in accordance with the sutta (yathāsuttaṃ); it means it explains whatever sutta in the way it should be explained. Or, 'yathāsuttaṃ' refers to whatever sutta, meaning all suttas. Indeed, there is no sutta that cannot be explained by the Netti method.## Now, regarding the statement 'The excellent Teaching should be known by the wise,' He said 'Yā ceva...' and so on to show the Pariyatti-dhamma itself, which is the object of the Netti commentary, by defining it in another way.## In that text, the sequence of phrasing with defined boundaries among meanings is called 'Desanā' (Teaching), and that sequence of phrasing is also called 'Pāṭha' (Text). Its meaning is called 'Desita' (What is taught), because it is made known by that Desanā. Both the Desanā and the Desita must certainly be known by those who practice with the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana) as the priority, as they are the cause of attainments ending in final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna). Or, because there is no object of knowledge (ñeyya) apart from these two, only these two should be known; this meaning is shown by the passage 'Yā ceva... viññeyyaṃ.' 'Tatra' (Therein) refers to that knowledge (vijānana) which is to be accomplished or produced; this locative case is used in the sense of the objective to be achieved. 'Ayamanupubbī' (This sequence) refers to this sequence of hāras and nayas to be mentioned; it means the hāras and nayas to be mentioned in order. 'Navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhi' means the search for the ninefold teaching (sāsana) by way of sutta etc., or the investigation of the meaning. Or this nominative case is in the sense of the possessive (sāmī-attha), meaning the sequence of the search for the meaning of the ninefold sutta. Alternatively, the nominative case in the word 'anupubbī' is in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa). This means: when the aforementioned knowledge is to be accomplished, this is the search for the meaning of the ninefold suttanta through the sequence of hāras and nayas to be mentioned.## Here, an objector asks: How can geyya and so on among these nine limbs be considered suttas? And if they are suttas, how can they be the nine limbs of the Teaching? In the commentaries (saṅgaha), it is said: 'A sutta with verses is geyya; a sutta without verses is veyyākaraṇa.' If that is so, then they would only be the sutta limb (suttaṅga)...
13: (The nine limbs) would not be [mutually exclusive]. If they were distinct sutta limbs, then the Maṅgala Sutta and others, being in verse, would not be included in the sutta limb, just like the Dhammapada and others; or they would be included in the geyya limb, like the Sagāthā-vagga, because they contain verses. Likewise, the verse portions in the Ubhatovibhaṅga etc. [would be included in geyya]. This being said, the answer is given:## 'Sutta' is a general rule; the others are specific rules. [The specific rules are distinguished] because they occur with a cause (nimitta), because they are well-known [in Maṅgala Sutta etc.], because they are associated with other verses [other than gujjhiya], and because they are not due to others [like verses in Ubhatovibhaṅga].## Calling the entire Buddha-word 'Sutta' is this general rule. For this reason, the term 'Sutta' is seen even in the specific categories of Vinaya, Abhidhamma, and Pariyatti, as in the statements: 'This much of the Blessed One's [teaching] has come in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta,' 'In the Suttavibhaṅga of Sāvatthī,' and 'Five hundred suttas in one's own doctrine.' However, in the parts of those suttas, geyya and so on are specific rules established by various causes. Thus, the presence of verses in geyya is the cause for it being the geyya limb. In the world also, people call a prose work (cuṇṇiyagantha) accompanied by gujjhiya verses 'geyya.' When verses are absent, the nature of questioning and answering is the [cause] for veyyākaraṇa. Questioning and answering itself is called 'byākaraṇa.' Byākaraṇa is the same as veyyākaraṇa.## If so, would not those teachings with verses also become veyyākaraṇa if they occur by way of questioning and answering? They would not, because they are not the domain of names like geyya, and because it is specified as 'when verses are absent.' Therefore, in the Dhammapada and others which are purely verse compositions, even though they have verses; and in specific suttas associated with verses consisting of joy and knowledge, or connected with phrases like 'This was said [by the Blessed One],' or connected with wonderful things (abbhutadhamma); the names Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and Abbhutadhamma are established respectively. Likewise, although they are in verse, the name Jātaka is established for suttas that reveal the conduct and power of the Blessed One in past lives. Although there is questioning and answering and the presence of verses, the name Vedalla is established in certain suttantas because they cause the attainment of wisdom. Thus, because the names geyya and so on are established in those specific suttas by various causes such as the presence of verses, geyya and so on are specific rules distinct from the sutta limb.## Among these [nine limbs], a sutta that is devoid of the causes for geyya etc. is called the sutta limb, because it proceeds by the general name, setting aside the specific names. If one objects: 'A sutta with verses is geyya, and a sutta without verses is veyyākaraṇa; therefore, a [distinct] sutta limb cannot exist,' does that objection not still stand? [The answer is:] That objection no longer stands because it has already been answered. It was already stated previously that the nature of questioning and answering in the absence of verses is the cause for veyyākaraṇa.
14:
If it is asked whether the objection—that a Sutta with verses is called Geyya and a Sutta without verses is called Veyyākaraṇa, and therefore Sutta-aṅga cannot exist—still stands, the answer is: No, it does not stand, because it has been cleared up. How was it cleared up? It was previously explained that even in the absence of verses, the nature of question and answer is the cause for being a Veyyākaraṇa-aṅga.

The statement that the Maṅgala Sutta and others should not be counted as Sutta-aṅga because they contain verses is also incorrect, because their status as Sutta is well-established. Indeed, the status of the Maṅgala Sutta and others as Sutta is well-known. These are not known by the status of verses like the Dhammapada or Buddhavamsa; rather, they are known only by the status of Sutta. For this very reason, the name "Sutta-nāmaka" (named Sutta) is used in the Commentary.

The statement that they should be counted as Geyya-aṅga because they contain verses is also incorrect, because they exist together with something else. Being "with verses" (sagāthaka) means being together with verses. Being "together with" means, in sense, being with something else. In the Maṅgala Sutta and others, there is no portion of the Sutta that is separate from the verses. Nor is there any collection called a Sutta that is said to be "together with verses."

The statement that the portions containing verses in the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others should be counted as Geyya-aṅga is also incorrect, because those are different verses. Those verses are different because they are included in the Jātakas and so on. Therefore, because of those verses, the Ubhatovibhaṅga and others do not have the status of Geyya-aṅga; thus, it should be understood that there is no mutual confusion between the aṅgas such as Sutta. However, since the entire Word of the Buddha is called Sutta because it indicates meanings in the manner already described, it is said: "The nine-fold Suttanta Pariyatti."

## The Explanation of the Chapter on Summary (Saṅgahavāra) is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Chapter on Synopsis (Uddesavāra)

Having thus shown the Hāras and others in brief through the Saṅgahavāra, the teaching beginning with "In that regard, what are the sixteen Hāras?" is now undertaken to show them in detail. In that teaching, "tatthā" (in that) refers to the statement "The sixteen Hāras are the Netti," or it means in those Hāras, Nayas, and Mūlapadas extracted from that verse. "Katame" (which) is a word of questioning. A question is of five kinds: a question to illuminate what is not seen (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā), a question to compare what is seen (diṭṭhasandandanā-pucchā), a question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā), a question to seek agreement (anumati-pucchā), and a question from a desire to speak/teach (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). Among these five, this question is one from a desire to teach. "Soḷasa" (sixteen) is a delimitation by number. By such delimitation, it shows the fact that these Hāras are exactly sixteen in extent, neither more nor less. This extent will become clear later. The word "Hārā" is a general term showing the Hāras delimited by number. The words "Desanā, Vicaya," etc., are the demonstration of their specific forms.

In this regard, the meaning of the component should be understood thus: For what reason are they called Hāras? They are called Hāras because, by these specific explanations, they remove ignorance (aññāṇa), doubt (samsaya), and perversion (vipallāsa) which have Sutta, Geyya, etc., as their objects. Or, they are called Hāras because they themselves remove [those things]. Or, they are called Hāras by metaphorical usage (phalūpacāra) because they are merely the act of removal.
15:
This (number of sixteen) shows the limit. This limit will become clear later. The word "Hāra" is a general term for the Hāras defined by number, while "Desanā, Vicaya," etc., show their specific characteristics. Among those (sixteen Hāras), for what reason are they called "Hāra"? They are called "Hāra" because, by these special commentaries or in these special commentaries, they remove ignorance (aññāṇa), doubt (samsaya), and perversion (vipallāsa) which have Sutta, Geyya, etc., as their objects. Or, they are called "Hāra" because they themselves remove that ignorance and so on, or because they are merely the act of removal, by way of metaphorical usage (phalūpacāra). Alternatively, they are called "Hāra" because they are spoken of by the person who teaches the Dhamma and the person who receives the Dhamma through the act of giving and receiving the Dhamma. Alternatively, they are called "Hāra" because they are like a jeweled necklace (hāra). How so? Just as a necklace, which is a collection of many jewels, produces great pleasure through the touch of its component jewels and allays the bodily heat of the wearer caused by the summer sun, so too these special commentaries, which are a sequence of various jewels of ultimate meaning, produce the bliss of peace through the attainment of the jewels of ultimate meaning that are their components, and allay the fever in the hearts of those who receive the Dhamma caused by defilements such as sensual lust (kāmarāga). Alternatively, they are called "Hāra" because they effect the removal (hāra) of ignorance and so on, or because they explain that removal. Alternatively, they are called "Hāra" by the method of Nirutti because they lead away (haraṇa) or delight (ramaṇa) the minds of the listeners. For example, it is said: "The Blessed One is called Bhagavā because he has gone to the end (vanta-gamana) of the three types of existence." This is the general (sādhāraṇa) meaning of the Hāras.

As for the specific (asādhāraṇa) meaning, it is called "Desanā" because the meaning of the Sutta is explained or commented upon by this [Hāra]. Or, it is called "Desanā" because it occurs together with the teaching (desanā). One might ask: Do not other Hāras also occur together with the teaching because they comment on the meaning of the Sutta called Desanā? That is true, but this Hāra deserves to be said to occur together with the teaching because it is mostly understood according to the literal sound (yathāruta), whereas others are not so. Indeed, there is no Sutta teaching devoid of the demonstration of gratification (assāda), danger (ādīnava), escape (nissaraṇa), and so on. And this Hāra has the characteristic of clarifying the demonstration of gratification and so on.

It is called "Vicaya" because words, questions, and so on are investigated by this [Hāra] or in this [Hāra], or because it is the investigation of those words and so on. In the Pāḷi, however, the meaning is shown as "Vicaya" because it investigates. "Yutti" is the nature of accomplishing according to the reason. In this context, however, the investigation of logic is called "Yutti." This is like calling the "fine-material existence" (rūpabhava) simply "fine-material" (rūpa) by dropping the latter word. Or, it is called "Yutti" because it occurs together with logic. In this Yutti-hāra, the meaning should be expanded in the same manner as stated in the Desanā-hāra.
16:
Padatthāna means the proximate cause. In this Hāra (mode of conveying), the investigation of the proximate cause and so forth should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

It is called the Lakkhaṇa Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, dhammas (phenomena) that have the same characteristic are taken by a single expression, even if they are not explicitly mentioned (in the Sutta).

It is called the Byūha Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, dhammas are gathered together by way of classification. It is called the Catubyūha Hāra because of the gathering of the four meanings such as nibbacana (etymological definition) and so forth shown in the Sutta, or because it is the gathering place of those four meanings.

It is called the Āvatta Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, similar (sabhāga) and dissimilar (visabhāga) dhammas are made to turn, or because of the turning of those dhammas.

It is called the Vibhatti Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, the planes (bhūmi) of the dhammas of defilement (saṅkilesa) and purification (vodāna), which are common (sādhāraṇa) and uncommon (asādhāraṇa), are analyzed. Alternatively, it is called the Vibhatti Hāra because of the analysis of the planes of those dhammas.

It is called the Parivattana Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, the dhammas taught in the Sutta are made to turn by way of opposites, or because of the turning of those dhammas.

It is called the Vivacana Hāra because in this Hāra, there are various words expressing a single meaning. Vivacana is the same as Vevacana (synonym). Alternatively, it is called the Vivacana Hāra because by this Hāra, the meaning is expressed in various ways. The remaining meanings should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

It is called the Paññatti Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, meanings are made known by way of variety or by way of distinction.

It is called the Otaraṇa Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, the dhammas appearing in the Sutta are made to enter (descend) into dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and so forth.

It is called the Sodhana Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, the words, the meanings of the words, the questions, and the introductions found in the Sutta are cleared (resolved).

It is called the Adhiṭṭhāna Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, dhammas that are general (sāmañña) and specific (visesa) are established (brought into being) as they are taught, without further conceptualization.

It is called Parikkhāra because it conditions the fruit; it is indeed the root-cause (hetu) and the condition (paccaya). It is called the Parikkhāra Hāra because it points out the parikkhāra (cause). It is called the Parikkhāra Hāra because it has parikkhāra as its scope or because it occurs together with parikkhāra.

It is called the Samāropana Hāra because by this Hāra, or in this Hāra, dhammas are properly attributed (superimposed) by taking the proximate cause (padatthāna) and so forth as the starting point. In all instances, since the meaning can also be established by way of the state of being (bhāvasādhana), it should be applied by way of that bhāvasādhana as well.
17:
'Tassa' refers to the previously mentioned summary of the Hāras (Hāruddesa). 'Anugīti' refers to the verses sung afterwards to make the previously mentioned meaning easy to remember. Among those verses, the concluding verse states 'unconfused by meaning' (asaṅkiṇṇa), which means there is no confusion in terms of the meaning of the words. Therefore, although some Hāras may appear as if they are not distinct from one another, it shows that there is no confusion between them in terms of meaning. This state of being unconfused is very clear in the Lakkhaṇaniddesa. 'Etesañceva' refers to these sixteen Hāras. Just as they are unconfused, they also exist in detail. How so? They exist in detail. 'Nayavibhatti' is the analysis by way of method (naya) or means (upāya). By this, that very state of being unconfused is made manifest. Some read it as 'vitthāranayā', but that reading is not good. This verse is not found in some palm-leaf manuscripts.

Having thus summarized the Hāras, now to summarize the methods (naya), 'Tattha katame' and so forth is stated. Therein, 'Naya' (Method) is so called because they make one known by analyzing the dhammas of defilement (saṅkilesa) and purification (vodāna). Alternatively, those dhammas are known by these methods, or are known in these methods. Or, they are called methods because they are merely the act of making known. Or, they are called methods because they are brought forward by the Dhamma preachers themselves to investigate the meaning of the Sutta. Alternatively, they are called methods because they are like methods. Indeed, if the methods such as unity (ekatta) and so forth are properly penetrated, they make known the nature of conventional truth (sammutisacca) and ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) without confusion by showing the sequence of causes and effects, their connection, their analysis, their lack of agency, and the corresponding result; thus they lead to the penetration of ultimate truth. Similarly, these methods such as Nandiyāvaṭṭa and so forth, by showing the analysis of dark (unwholesome), bright (wholesome), and opposite dhammas, succeed in providing the realization of the unerring meaning of the Sutta, and thus lead to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths by those to be led (veneyya). Alternatively, according to the etymological method (nirutti-naya), they are called Naya because they lead to (nayana) the meaning of the scriptures (pariyatti) and because they restrain (yamana) one from the dhammas of defilement.

In the terms such as Nandiyāvaṭṭa and so forth, it is called Nandiyāvaṭṭa because it has a turning like the turning of a Nandiyāvaṭṭa flower (jasmine). Just as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa flower turns outwards from its central principal part, so this method turns outwards by its principal parts, namely craving (taṇhā), ignorance (avijjā), tranquility (samatha), and insight (vipassanā). Alternatively, it is called Nandiyāvaṭṭa because in this method, there is the turning of craving (nandi) or of joy. It is called Tipukkhala (Threefold Excellence) because it is beautiful due to the three components from the side of defilement such as greed (lobha) and so forth, and the three components from the side of purification such as non-greed (alobha) and so forth. The Blessed One is called a Lion (Sīha) because He is endowed with special qualities such as fearlessness, speed, and effort. His dwelling, which is the verbal action of teaching, is called 'play' (vikkīḷita). Because it shows the perversions (vippallāsa) and their opposites, it is said that in this method, there is the play of the Buddha who is like a lion; thus it is called Sīhavikkīḷita.
18:
It is the mode named Sīhavikkīḷita (The Lion's Play). This mode is called Sīhavikkīḷita either because it demonstrates the association with special powers or because it resembles the play of a lion. Here, 'special powers' refers to the five powers (balas) such as faith (saddhā) or the ten powers (dasabala) themselves. The looking at dhammas such as the wholesome (kusala) by way of the triad of meanings and modes is called Disālocana (Surveying the Directions). Because it properly leads those dhammas thus surveyed into the triad of meanings and modes, it is called Aṅkusa (The Goad), like a goad. Because it clarifies the meaning of the Sutta in the verses, it is called Lanjaka (The Clarifier); and since that mode is also a clarifier, it is called Nayalanjaka. 'Gatā' means they are known; 'matā' has the same meaning. Alternatively, 'matā' is the original reading. The rest should be understood in the manner already stated.

Having thus briefly shown the modes, the text "Tattha katamāni" etc. is undertaken to briefly show the root-terms (mūlapada). In that Pali, they are 'roots' (mūla) because they are the foundation for the modes and the analytical divisions of the Teaching (sāsanapaṭṭhāna); they are 'terms' (pada) because they are the means of attainment and represent specific portions. Therefore, they are called 'mūlapadāni' (root-terms). They are called 'wholesome' (kusala) because they are born of wisdom, or because they destroy loathsome unwholesome states, or because they cut off loathsome greed and so on, or because they cut like kusa grass, or because they are to be proceeded with by means of wisdom (kusa). They are called 'unwholesome' (akusala) because they are the opposite of the wholesome. Thus the meaning of the terms should be understood.

Having thus shown the root-terms by way of number and by way of class, now wishing to show them by way of their nature, the Teacher first briefly shows the side of defilement (saṃkilesa) with the words "Taṇhā" etc. Therein, it is called 'taṇhā' (craving) because it thirsts. It is called 'avijjā' (ignorance) because it takes up unwholesome conduct which should not be taken, and does not take up wholesome conduct which should be taken; or because it is the opposite of knowledge (vijjā). It is called 'lobha' (greed) because one lusts by means of that nature, or it lusts by itself, or it is merely the state of lusting. The same method applies to hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). The perception that occurs as "beautiful" in the foul (asubha) is called 'subhasaññā' (perception of beauty). The meaning of 'sukhasaññā' (perception of pleasure) etc. should be understood by this same method. 'Saṅgaha' means counting. 'Samosaraṇa' means gathering together.

It is called 'samatha' (tranquility) because it calms opposing states. It is called 'vipassanā' (insight) because it sees in various ways such as impermanence (anicca). Non-greed (alobha) and so on should be understood as the opposites of greed and so on. The perception that occurs as "foul" in the foul is called 'asubhasaññā' (perception of foulness); it is indeed the foundation of mindfulness of body (kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna). This is because the teaching is given with perception as the heading. The same method applies to 'dukkhasaññā' (perception of suffering) etc.

"Idaṃ uddānaṃ" means it is called 'uddāna' (summary) because it guards from above to prevent the aforementioned meanings from becoming scattered and lost; the meaning is a summary statement. "Cattāro
19:
There is also the reading "vipallāsā". The ground of defilements (kilesabhūmi) is called the ground of corruption (saṃkilesabhūmi) because it is the place of convergence for all unwholesome states. There are those three roots of the wholesome. They also read "kusalāni". 'Satipaṭṭhānā' is said in reference to the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā) and so on. It is called the ground of faculties (indriyabhūmi) because it is the place of convergence for the faculties such as faith (saddhā) which ripen liberation (vimutti). 'Yujjanti' means they are joined. The word "kho" is an expletive (padapūraṇa) or a particle in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). By that word "kho", it shows that 'only these' such as craving are the root-terms. Or it shows that 'only eighteen' terms are the root-terms. 'Mūlapadā' is 'mūlapadāni', or it is a change of gender.

## End of the Description of the Summary Section.

## 3. Description of the Explanatory Section

Having thus briefly shown the modes of conveyance (hāra) and so on, the text "Tattha saṅkhepato" etc. is undertaken to explain them in detail. In that text, 'tattha' means in that summary text (uddesapāṭha). "Saṅkhepato netti kittitā" means the Nettippakaraṇa has been told in brief. This is because the demonstration of the nature of the modes of conveyance (hāra), modes (naya), and root-terms (mūlapada) was done by the summary text. Here, regarding the hāras and nayas—

The wise should know the meaning of the terms, the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), the order (kama), the extent of this much, and the causes (hetu) etc., by way of both the general and the specific.

Among those meanings of terms etc., the meaning of the hāras and nayas has been shown generally and specifically. As for the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) etc., generally all hāras and nayas have the characteristic of explaining the meaning of the nine-fold Teaching of the Teacher (navanga-satthu-sāsana) by way of phrasing and meaning in due order. Specifically, however, we shall state the characteristic of each hāra and naya only in the Explanatory Section (Niddesavāra). Since the order (kama) and so on are easily understood only after their characteristics are known, we shall also clarify those orders etc. after the Explanatory Section.

## Summary of the Modes of Conveyance

There are explanatory verses (niddesagāthā) beginning with "Yā pana assādādīnavatā" etc. In those verses, "assādādīnavatā" is divided into the terms "assādo" and "ādīnavatā". "Ādīnavatā" is just "ādīnava" (danger). Some read "assādādīnavato"; that reading is not good. In that text, it is called 'assāda' (gratification) because it is enjoyed; it is pleasure (sukha) and joy (somanassa). For it has been said: "Bhikkhus, whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on the five aggregates of clinging, this is the gratification (assāda) in the five aggregates of clinging."
20: "Gratification (assāda) in the aggregates that are the objects of clinging" is stated. Just as this happiness (sukha) and joy (somanassa) are called gratification, so too is a pleasant object (iṭṭhārammaṇa). It is also taught: "He finds gratification in that object, he desires it"; "He finds gratification in the form-object, he greatly delights in it, and based on that form-object, lust arises"; and "Monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are fetters (craving increases)." Alternatively, craving (taṇhā) is called gratification because one finds gratification through this craving. Because of craving, which is the root cause, a person finds gratification in happiness and in happy objects. Like craving, perversions (vipallāsa) are also called gratification. By the power of perversion, beings find gratification even in unpleasant objects as if they were pleasant. Thus, the analysis of gratification in feeling, in all formations of the three planes, in craving, and in perversions should be understood. How can painful (dukkha) feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant (adukkhamasukha) feeling be objects of gratification? It is possible through perversion and because they have the nature of being a synonym for happiness. Thus it is taught: "Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is pleasant when it persists and painful when it changes. Painful feeling is painful when it persists and pleasant when it changes. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant when there is knowledge and painful when there is no knowledge." Among those things of gratification, the analysis should be understood: feeling by way of the 108 modes; formations of the three planes by way of the Nikkhēpakaṇḍa and Rūpakaṇḍa; craving by way of the Saṅkilesavatthuvibhaṅga and the description of craving in the Nikkhēpakaṇḍa; and perversions by way of the perception of happiness, etc., and by way of the sixty-two types of wrong view. Danger (ādīnava) is painful feeling, or the three types of suffering (dukkha-dukkhatā, saṅkhāra-dukkhatā, vipariṇāma-dukkhatā) are called danger. Or all formations of the three planes are called danger. It is called danger because it leads to extreme misery (kapaṇa); like a miserable person, the things of the three planes have such a nature because they are associated with impermanence and so on. Therefore, it is called the method of knowing according to reality for those practitioners of insight who have begun the contemplation of danger in those things. Thus it is taught: "Monks, that the five aggregates of clinging are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the five aggregates of clinging." Therefore, danger should be pointed out by analyzing it by way of birth and so on, which are the descriptions of the truth of suffering, and by way of the forty-two modes such as impermanence. The Noble Path is called escape (nissaraṇa) because one escapes (from saṃsāra) by means of this Noble Path. Or Nibbāna is called escape because it is the place of escape (from saṃsāra). By expressing both generally or by the method of ellipsis (ekasesa)...
21: ...it is called "escape" (nissaraṇa). The word "pi" (also) has the meaning of connecting the preceding and following statements. Therein, regarding the side of the Noble Path, escape should be pointed out by analyzing it by way of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment such as the foundations of mindfulness, and by way of the divisions included in that path such as the contemplation of the body. Regarding the side of Nibbāna, although there is no division in the ultimate sense because it is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), it is analyzed figuratively by way of Nibbāna with residue (saupādisesa-nibbāna) and Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). Alternatively, that Nibbāna is the escape from certain things; it should be pointed out by analyzing it as the state of escape from conditioned things such as: the six doors like the eye as shown in the Paṭisambhidāmagga; the six objects like forms; the six types each of consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, craving, initial application, and sustained application occurring at those respective doors; the six elements like the earth element; the ten kasina bases; the foul things (asubha); the thirty-two parts of the body like hair; the five aggregates; the twelve sense bases; the eighteen elements; the mundane faculties; the three elements like the sense-sphere element; the three types of existence like sense-sphere existence; the four jhānas; the illimitables (appamaññā); the immaterial jhānas; and the twelve factors of dependent origination. "Fruit" (phala) refers to the fruit of the teaching (desanā-phala). What is that fruit? It is the result accomplished through the teaching. One might ask: "Is it not the case that the attainment of Nibbāna is accomplished through the teaching of the Buddha, and has Nibbāna not already been mentioned by the word 'escape' (nissaraṇa)?" That is true, but that Nibbāna is accomplished only through a sequence (paramparā). Here, however, the fruit of the teaching is intended in the sense of immediate realization (paccakkha). That fruit is the knowledge consisting in what is heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa). It consists of the six purifications (visuddhi) which are the practices in the preliminary stage of the Noble Path, such as knowing the meaning and knowing the text. For one who cannot yet attain the Path at that moment (of hearing the teaching), it can also be the cause of a fortunate rebirth (sampatti-bhava) which becomes the cause for attaining that Path in the future. Thus (the teacher Kaccāyana) will say: "Having removed the view of self, one should thus cross over death"—this statement is the fruit (phala); "The Dhamma indeed protects the one who practices the Dhamma"—this statement is the fruit (phala). In this way, among devas and humans, the accomplishments (sampatti) of long life, beauty, strength, happiness, fame, retinue, and sovereignty, as well as the accomplishments of the physical body (upadhi-sampatti), the glory of a universal monarch, the glory of a king of devas, the four wheels of fortune, the accomplishment of virtue, the accomplishment of concentration, the three knowledges, the six direct knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, the enlightenment of a disciple, the enlightenment of a private Buddha, and the supreme enlightenment—all these accomplishments, having the accumulation of merit as their cause, should be understood as "fruit" (phala) because they are to be achieved through the teaching of the Buddha.
22:
Upāya refers to the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipadā) which is the proximate cause of the Noble Path. This is because the preceding practice serves as the means for attaining the succeeding practice, and sequentially, it is the cause for the attainment of the Path and Nibbāna; thus it is called 'upāya' (means). The practice which is the means for attaining the previously mentioned fruit (phala) is also called upāya. Some teachers, however, say: "The Path together with insight is called upāya." According to their view, the term 'nissaraṇa' (escape) would refer only to Nibbāna. Just like the fruit, upāya would also be referred to as the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). It can be understood that even in the words Venerable Kaccāyana will state later, "All phenomena... for purification, this is the upāya," only the preliminary practice is being presented. In fact, with the words "Having abandoned them, one should cross the flood," Venerable Kaccāyana will state that the Noble Path is the escape (nissaraṇa). Therefore, the term 'nissaraṇa' does not refer only to Nibbāna, but also to the Path. This is because the Noble Path is the crossing of the flood (oghataraṇa).

Āṇatti (Instruction) refers to the command or exhortation "Practice thus" given by the Blessed One, who is worthy of commanding, for the welfare and success of those to be led (veneyya). Thus, he will state later: "Look upon the world as empty, Mogharāja; this is the āṇatti."

'Yogīnaṃ' (of the practitioners) means for the sake of those to be led who are intensely devoted to the development of the meditation on the Four Truths; the words 'for the sake of' should be added as a completion of the sentence. Desanāhāra (The Mode of Conveying a Teaching) is a specific explanation characterized by the analysis of the aforementioned gratification (assāda) and so on. Here, a question may arise: "Is the complete statement of these gratifications, etc., the Desanāhāra, or is it the statement of only some?" Only the complete statement is called Desanāhāra. In a Sutta where gratification (assāda), danger (ādīnava), and escape (nissaraṇa) appear in their own form, there is nothing further to be said. However, where they appear only partially or not in their own form, the hāra (mode) must be applied by extracting the unmentioned meaning according to the sense. Since this matter will appear in the Desanāhāravibhaṅga, it is not elaborated here.

'Yaṃ pucchitaṃ' (that which is questioned) refers to the question (pucchā); the words 'is investigated' should be added as a completion. In the phrase 'vissajjitaṃ anugīti' (the answer and the subsequent verse), the same method applies (the words 'is investigated' should be understood). Therein, 'vissajjitaṃ' refers to the answer (vissajjanā). That answer is of four kinds through the power of categorical explanation (ekaṃsavyākaraṇa), etc. The word 'ca' (and) has the sense of aggregation. By that word 'ca', terms not mentioned in the verse are included. If it is asked, "Of what are these questions and answers?", it is said 'suttassa' (of the Sutta). By this, it is shown that the questions and answers appearing in the Sutta must be investigated. 'Yā ca anugīti' refers to the summary verse (saṅgahagāthā) which is a subsequent recital (anugīti) of the meaning already stated in the Sutta. Or, it is a recital corresponding to the question. By this term 'anugīti', the sequence (pubbāpara) is taken. The answer being consistent with the question is intended as the sequence (pubbāpara) in this Vicayahāra. That consistency with the question is called 'pucchānusandhi'. The preceding word 'suttassa' is a word that relates to the preceding words 'pucchita' and 'vissajjita'. Therefore, 'suttassa' is stated again. By that latter word 'suttassa', the gratification (assāda), etc., which arise depending on the Sutta, are encompassed. To this extent, the scope of the Vicayahāra has been completely shown.
23:
The sequence (pubbāpara) is taken. In this Vicayahāra, the consistency of the answer with the question is intended as 'pubbāpara'. That consistency with the question is called 'pucchānusandhi'. The preceding word 'suttassa' is stated again because it relates to the preceding words 'pucchita' and 'vissajjita'. By that (latter) word 'suttassa', the gratification (assāda), etc., which are the basis of the Sutta, are encompassed. To this extent, the scope of the Vicayahāra is shown without remainder. Being thus shown, it will be stated in the Vicayahāravibhaṅga: "He investigates the term... he investigates the subsequent verse."

Among those (eleven items such as terms and questions), the sequential investigation of all terms appearing in the Sutta by way of meaning and by way of phrasing is called Padavicaya (Investigation of Terms). "This question is an adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā (a question illuminating an unseen meaning), a diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā (a question comparing a seen meaning), a vimaticchedanā-pucchā (a question cutting off doubt), an anumati-pucchā (a question seeking agreement), a kathetukamyatā-pucchā (a question asked with the desire to preach), a sattādhiṭṭhānā-pucchā (a question based on beings), a dhammādhiṭṭhānā-pucchā (a question based on phenomena), an ekādhiṭṭhānā-pucchā (a question based on a single thing), an anekādhiṭṭhānā-pucchā (a question based on many things), a sammutivisaya-pucchā (a question concerning conventional reality), a paramatthavisaya-pucchā (a question concerning ultimate reality), an atێتavisaya-pucchā (a question concerning the past), an anāgatavisaya-pucchā (a question concerning the future), a paccuppannavisaya-pucchā (a question concerning the present)"—thus should Pucchāvicaya (Investigation of Questions) be understood. "This answer is an ekaṃsavyākaraṇa (a categorical explanation), a vibhajjavyākaraṇa (an analytical explanation), a paṭipucchāvyākaraṇa (an explanation by counter-question), a ṭhapanā (an explanation by setting aside), sāvasesa (with remainder), niravasesa (without remainder), sauttara (surpassable), anuttara (unsurpassable), lokiya (mundane), lokuttara (supramundane)"—thus should Vissajjanavicaya (Investigation of Answers) be understood.

"This question is consistent with this answer, it is not consistent with that answer"—the investigation by bringing forward the questioned meaning, as well as the investigation by comparing the preceding and following words, is called Pubbāparavicaya (Investigation of Sequence). "This subsequent verse is a vuttatthasaṅgaha (a summary of the stated meaning), an avuttatthasaṅgaha (a summary of the unstated meaning), a tadubhayatthasaṅgaha (a summary of both), a kusalatthasaṅgaha (a summary of wholesome meaning), an akusalatthasaṅgaha (a summary of unwholesome meaning)"—thus should Anugītivicaya (Investigation of Subsequent Verses) be understood. Among gratification (assāda), etc., the extraction of specific meanings of gratification through the power of terms found in the 22 triads and 142 dyads, such as defining pleasant feeling as "having the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object," craving as "having the characteristic of grasping an object," perversions (vipallāsa) as "having the characteristic of distorted grasping," and the remaining phenomena of the three planes as "having their respective characteristics," is called Assādavicaya (Investigation of Gratification).

Defining painful feeling as "having the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object," the truths of suffering as "having the characteristic of rebirth," and impermanence, etc., as "impermanent" because of having a beginning and an end and because of having an end in impermanence—the investigation of danger (ādīnava) is understood by extracting the inferior nature in the occurrence of danger through the power of factors like being part of defilement or part of decline for all mundane phenomena. In the term 'escape' (nissaraṇa), of the Noble Path...
24:
Investigation (vicaya) should be understood by way of the terms to be obtained in all states of gratification (assāda), in the twenty-two triads (tika), and in the one hundred and forty-two dyads (duka). The extraction of the specific meaning of each gratification is called the investigation of gratification (assāda-vicaya). Investigation of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) should be understood as 'having the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object,' and so forth. Investigation of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) should be understood as 'having the characteristic of being reborn,' and so forth. Investigation of impermanence (anicca) and so forth should be understood as 'they are impermanent' because of having a beginning and an end, or because of having an end that is not permanent. Investigation of all mundane states (lokiya-dhamma) should be understood by way of having the part of defilement, the part of decline, and so forth. In the occurrence of danger (ādīnava), the investigation of danger (ādīnava-vicaya) should be understood by extracting the inferior aspect.

In the term 'escape' (nissaraṇa), the investigation of escape (nissaraṇa-vicaya) should be understood by way of extracting the distinction of the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) such as contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), which is the cause for the Noble Path (ariya-magga), and by way of extracting the distinction of Nibbāna through the aforementioned methods (pariyāya). Investigation (vicaya) should be understood by way of extracting and defining the fruit (phala) to be accomplished in various sutta discourses, the means (upāya) to that fruit, and the prescriptive words (vidhāna-vacana) of the Buddha in those various instances. Thus, the 'Mode of Investigation' (vicaya-hāra) should be understood as having the characteristic of investigation solely by way of extracting the distinctions in the questioning and answering of terms, the sequences (anugīti), and gratification (assāda), etc.

'Sabbesaṃ' refers to the sixteen modes (hāra). 'Bhūmi' (ground) is said with reference to phrasing (byañjana). Phrasing is the ground or the place of occurrence for the methods (naya) and the modes (hāra), just like the root terms; this is because those modes have the nature of examining the phrasing. Indeed, it has been said: 'The modes are the investigation of phrasing.' In the Peṭaka also, it is said: 'Where all the modes, arriving together, lead to the meaning of the sutta, because of the variety of the ways of phrasing.' 'Gocara' (domain) refers to the meaning of the sutta (suttattha). This is because the application of the modes is based on the extraction of the meaning of the terms in the sutta. The examination of the suitability or unsuitability of those phrasings and meanings is called 'yuttāyutta-parikkhā'. There is also a variant reading 'yuttāyutti-parikkhā', which means the investigation of suitability (yutti) and unsuitability.

How can the suitability or unsuitability of those phrasings and meanings be known? It can be known by non-contradiction with the four Great Authorities (mahāpadesa). Therein, for phrasing (byañjana), being the natural linguistics (sabhāva-nirutti) and being able to express the intended meaning is the state of suitability (yutta-bhāva). For the meaning (attha), it is the non-contradiction with the Sutta, the Vinaya, and the nature of things (dhammatā). This is a summary here. The detail will be made clear later. As it is pointed out that 'the mode is suitability,' the 'Mode of Construing' (yutti-hāra) should be understood as having the characteristic of clarifying the suitability or unsuitability of the phrasing and meaning in a sutta.
