It is not only the fourth base of power (iddhipāda) that is rooted in the knowledge of concentration; rather, to show that all bases of power are rooted in the knowledge of concentration, it was said: "All concentration is rooted in knowledge, preceded by knowledge, and follows knowledge." If that is so, why is only that fourth base of power called the concentration of investigation (vīmaṃsā-samādhi)? The intended meaning is that it is so called because it is practiced by making investigation (wisdom) the leader. In that statement, it is rooted in knowledge through preliminary wisdom (pubbabhāga-paññā). It is preceded by knowledge through attainment wisdom (adhigama-paññā). It follows knowledge through reviewing wisdom (paccavekkhaṇa-paññā). Alternatively, it is rooted in knowledge through preliminary wisdom; it is preceded by knowledge through access wisdom (upacāra-paññā); and it follows knowledge through absorption wisdom (appanā-paññā). Or else, it should be understood that it is rooted in knowledge through access wisdom; it is preceded by knowledge through absorption wisdom; and it follows knowledge through direct-knowledge wisdom (abhiññā-paññā).

"As in the past" means: just as there is nothing difficult to penetrate—whether it be the aggregates of oneself or others, or things connected to the aggregates such as names and lineages—in the many past lives or in the incalculable aeons of contraction and expansion, because concentration follows the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbe-nivāsānussati-ñāṇa); so too, "in the future" means: there is nothing difficult to penetrate—whether it be the aggregates of oneself or others, or things connected to the aggregates—in the lives to come or in the incalculable aeons of contraction and expansion, because concentration follows the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa).

"As in the future" means: just as there is nothing difficult to penetrate regarding the minds of other beings in the seven days of the future, because concentration follows the knowledge of discerning the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa); so too, "in the past" means: there is nothing difficult to penetrate regarding the minds of other beings in the seven days of the past. "As by day" means: just as during the day, because darkness is dispelled by the light of the sun, visible forms that come into range are easily known by beings with eyesight; so too, "by night" means: even when darkness endowed with the four factors is present, there is no visible-form base (rūpāyatana) that is difficult to penetrate, because concentration follows the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa).

"As by night, so by day" means: just as by night, so too by day, there is nothing difficult to penetrate among all visible forms, whether they be extremely subtle, concealed by something, or located at a great distance. Just as it was stated regarding the visible-form base, the same should be applied to the sound base (saddāyatana), because concentration follows the knowledge of the divine ear (dibba-sota-ñāṇa). Therefore, it was said: "Thus with a mind that is open," and so on. In that passage, "unobstructed" (apariyonaddha) means not overwhelmed by the defilements that hinder direct-knowledge (abhiññā). Precisely because it is unobstructed, the mind is luminous. By this, it should be understood that the fact that concentration follows the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa) is also stated. "The five faculties" refers to the five faculties of a trainee (sekha) that are associated with the bases of power.
73:
The commentator says "kusalāni" (wholesome/skilled). The phrase beginning with "cittasahabhūni" is initiated (stated) to show how those faculties cease due to the cessation of consciousness. Likewise, the phrase beginning with "nāmarūpañca" is also stated to show cessation through the cessation of consciousness. By this, it is shown: "It is not only the five faculties that cease due to the cessation of consciousness; rather, name-and-form, which has consciousness as its cause, also ceases due to the cessation of consciousness."

"Tassa" refers to consciousness. "Hetu" refers to craving (taṇhā), ignorance (avijjā), and so on. The word "anāhāraṃ" (without nutriment) is an explanation of the meaning of that term. "Anabhinanditaṃ" (not delighted in) means not longed for, precisely because craving, which has the nature of delighting, has been abandoned. Because craving has been abandoned in this way, that consciousness, which is without rebirth-linking (appaṭisandhika), ceases. Just as consciousness ceases due to the absence of cause, so too name-and-form is without cause and without condition, because the cause and condition called consciousness is absent, and because the conditions such as volitional formations (saṅkhāra) which have that consciousness as their cause are absent. The rest is clear. The analysis of the questions and answers should also be understood according to the method already stated.

Having thus shown the question by way of connection (anusandhi), and since the questions based on persons (sattādhiṭṭhāna) and questions based on states (dhammādhiṭṭhāna) were shown separately below, the phrase beginning with "ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse" is now initiated to show them together. Therein, this is the meaning of the terms: "Saṅkhātadhammā" is a designation for Arahants whose states have been thoroughly investigated by way of impermanence and so on. "Sekkhā" refers to the remaining noble persons (ariya-puggala) who are still training in virtue and so on. "Puthū" refers to the many (seven types of) persons. "Tesaṃ me nipako iriyaṃ, puṭṭho pabrūhi" means: "O Wise Blessed One, please tell me, who am asking, about the conduct of those trainees (sekha) and non-trainees (asekha/Arahants)." The rest can be understood according to the Pali text itself.

"Kissa" means for what reason, or why. "Sekhāsekha-vipassanā-pubbaṅgama-pahāna-yogena" means by way of the questioning method associated with the trainees and non-trainees, and with the abandonings preceded by insight (vipassanā).

In the verse of the answer, "kāmesu nābhigijjheyya" means one should not be greedy for the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthu-kāma) by way of the defilement of sensuality (kilesa-kāma). "Manasānāvilo siyā" means one should be undisturbed in mind, abandoning states that cause the mind to be disturbed, such as thoughts of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) and bodily misconduct. Because the non-trainee (Arahant) is skilled in all states because they have been weighed by way of impermanence and so on, is mindful in all states through the mindfulness of body-contemplation (kāyānupassanā-sati) and so on, and has reached the state of a supreme monk because all defilements have been destroyed, he proceeds (dwells) in all postures. Therefore, it was said: "The skilled one... (pe)... should wander." This is the summary of the meaning.
74:
In those verses of inquiry (pucchā-gāthā) and verses of answer (vissajjanā-gāthā), the word 'nipaka' (prudent) is spoken in reference to the Blessed One. Because the Blessed One's wisdom, which has reached the highest perfection, should be demonstrated through unobstructed knowledge and vision (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa-dassana), the passage beginning with 'bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ' (all bodily actions of the Blessed One...) is stated to show the practice of the trainee (sekha) and the one beyond training (asekha) by first analyzing that unobstructed knowledge according to the divisions of the doors of action (kamma-dvāra).

By that unobstructed knowledge and vision in all respects, it clarifies only the Tathāgata's skill in teaching the practice of the trainee and the one beyond training. In that context, 'ko ca' means 'in what object' or 'in what domain'. That domain is shown by the phrase 'yaṃ anicce dukkhe anattani ca' (that which is in the impermanent, the suffering, and the non-self). This means that when the so-called knowledge and vision arises, it arises as: 'All conditioned things are impermanent and suffering; all phenomena are non-self.' The non-occurrence of that knowledge and vision in that domain due to non-knowing and non-seeing is called 'paṭighāta' (obstruction). By this, it shows the difficulty of penetrating the three characteristics (lakkhaṇattaya) and that this is unique to the Buddha, not shared with others. By the clarification of the three characteristics, the wise acknowledge the Blessed One's penetration of the Four Noble Truths and his Supreme Enlightenment.

By the words 'aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ' (non-knowing, non-seeing), that obstruction is shown in its own nature. Indeed, delusion (sammoha), which covers the nature of the six sense objects, is the obstruction to knowledge and vision. Since the obstruction of that knowledge must exist only in the domain where knowledge and vision are worthy of arising, it is said: 'yaṃ anicce dukkhe anattani ca'. The passage beginning with 'yatha idha puriso' (just as a man here...) is an illustration by way of a simile. Here is the comparison of the simile: The man is like the world of sentient beings (sattaloka); the collection of stars is like the six sense objects; that man's seeing of the stars is like the worldlings' knowing of the six sense objects accordingly through eye-consciousness and so on; and just as that man, even while seeing the stars, does not know them by way of counting or designation as 'this many hundreds, this many thousands', so too worldlings, even though they know the objects such as visible forms in some manner, do not understand the three characteristics such as impermanence. The rest of the words are clear.

Now, to analyze the meaning of the words by which the Blessed One spoke of the practice of the trainee and the one beyond training to the Venerable Ajita, the passage beginning with 'tattha sekhena' is stated. In that context, 'tattha' is merely a particle, or it means 'in that answer'. Regarding 'sekhena': one whose habit is training (sikkhā) is a 'sekha' (trainee); thus, 'by that trainee'. 'Dvīsu dhammesu' means in two kinds of states. 'Pariyuṭṭhānīyesu' means in those grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu) where one should be moved by obsessive anger; this is the meaning. There is also a reading 'paṭighaṭṭhānīyesu', which has the same meaning.
75:
In this exhortation regarding the prohibition of greed (gedha), it is stated by extracting that the mind must also be protected from anger (dosa), because anger rooted in greed occurs when greed is present. However, since the Blessed One said, "One should not be greedy for sensual pleasures," the detailed explanation (niddesa) is made by way of greed, starting with "In those sensual pleasures, whatever desire..." Alternatively, it should be understood that the necessity of protecting the mind from anger is already stated by the second line of the verse. For by the second line, all states of purification (vodāna-dhamma) from the remaining defilements are shown.

In showing this, because it is the domain of Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma) according to the division of arisen and unarisen states, all states of defilement and purification are analyzed into four parts. To show the practice of the trainee reaching its peak by means of the Right Exertions (sammappadhāna), the passage beginning with 'sekho abhigijjhanto' is stated. In that statement, 'anāvila-saṅkappo' (unpolluted thought) means having thoughts that are not turbid due to the absence of turbid sensual thoughts and so on. For that very reason, being one who is not greedy, he strives and exerts energy. To show how he strives, it is said: 'so anuppannānaṃ' and so forth.

In that statement, 'so' (he) refers to the trainee (sekha) who practices for the sake of attaining the higher distinction. 'Anuppannānaṃ' means those that have not yet arisen. 'Pāpakānaṃ' means evil or inferior. 'Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ' means states born of lack of skill (unwholesome states). 'Anuppādāya' means for the sake of non-arising. 'Chandaṃ janeti' means he generates wholesome desire, known as the desire to act (kattukamyatā). 'Vāyamati' means he makes an effortful endeavor. 'Viriyaṃ ārabhati' means he exerts bodily and mental energy. 'Cittaṃ paggaṇhāti' means he upholds the mind with that co-nascent energy. 'Padahati' means he performs the supreme exertion. The four terms beginning with 'vāyamati', however, should be applied to repetition, development, frequent practice, and constant action.

'Uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ' means those evil states that have reached the state where they cannot be called unarisen (i.e., arisen states). 'Pahānāya' means for the sake of abandoning. 'Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ' means those states born of skill (wholesome states) that have not yet arisen. 'Uppādāya' means for the sake of arising. 'Uppannānaṃ' means those that have arisen. 'Ṭhitiyā' means for the sake of duration. 'Asammosāya' means for the sake of non-disappearance. 'Bhiyyobhāvāya' means for the sake of repeated occurrence. 'Vepullāya' means for the sake of abundance. 'Bhāvanāya' means for the sake of increase. 'Pāripūriyā' means for the sake of fulfillment. This is the word-by-word meaning.

16. The passage beginning with 'katame anuppannā' (which are the unarisen...) is undertaken to show what kind of unwholesome and wholesome states are unarisen and what kind are arisen. In that statement, 'ime anuppannā' (these are unarisen) refers to these thoughts of sensual pleasure (kāma-vitakka) and so on, whether by way of non-occurrence...
76:
Alternatively, states are called "unrisen" (anuppanna) by way of objects that have not yet been experienced. Otherwise, in the beginningless Saṃsāra, there are no unwholesome states (akusala dhamma) that have never arisen. In showing these unrisen unwholesome states, the inclusion of the three thoughts (vitakka) should be understood merely as an illustration. The term "unwholesome roots" (akusalamūla) is used because the latent tendencies (anusaya) alone are the root cause of all unwholesome states; it does not refer only to greed (lobha) and so on. These arisen (uppanna) latent tendencies are called "arisen" only by name, because they possess the modes of arising such as "having gained a footing" (bhūmiladdhuppanna) and "not yet uprooted" (asamugghāṭituppanna); it does not mean they are manifest in the present (vattamāna-bhāva).

"These unrisen wholesome states" (anuppanna kusala dhamma) means that for a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala), the states such as faith (saddhā) belonging to a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) are called unrisen wholesome states; it is shown that there is no need to mention worldlings (puthujjana) (for whom it is obvious). Here too, the word "wholesome" (kusala) should be understood in the sense of "blameless" (anavajja), as in the Bāhitika Sutta. "These arisen wholesome states" means that for a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of Stream-entry, the states such as faith in the first path (pathama-magga) are called arisen wholesome states.

Sensual thought (kāma-vitakka) is well-restrained by the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā); therefore, it is said: "That by which one restrains sensual thought is the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya)." Ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), which arises depending on mental suffering and is a cause of distraction, is well-restrained by non-distraction (concentration) which has blameless happiness as its proximate cause; therefore, it is said: "That by which one restrains ill-will is the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya)." A person who has aroused energy (vīriya) in wholesome states can easily endure the faults of others; therefore, it is meant that cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka) is well-restrained by energy, and it is said: "That by which one restrains cruelty is the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya)." To show that the abandoning of the respective opposites of concentration and so on is accomplished only for the wise, it is said: "That by which, as they repeatedly arise..." and so on.

To show the supremacy (jeṭṭhaka-bhāva) of these five faculties as defined in their respective domains, it is said: "Where is the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) to be seen?" and so on. That is easily understood. Intending to show that through the accomplishment of these faculties such as faith, which belong to trainees (sekha), all trainee-states reach their summit, the practice of the trainee (sekha-paṭipadā) is concluded with the words: "Thus the trainee..." and so on.

Having thus analyzed the practice of the trainee, the text now says: "Skilled in all states..." and so on, to analyze the practice of the non-trainee (asekha-paṭipadā). In that passage, having first analyzed the states mentioned by the term "in all states" (sabba-dhamma), it is said: "What is called the world..." and so on, to show the skill of the non-trainee in those states.
77:
"What is called the world" (loko nāma) and so on has been said. That has the same meaning as previously stated. "The world of existence (bhava-loka) arises through the world of defilements (kilesa-loka)" means that depending on the sense-sphere states (kāmāvacara-dhamma), one brings about the fine-material and immaterial sphere states (rūpa-arūpāvacara-dhamma). "He" (so) refers to that person established in lofty states (mahaggata-dhamma) or in both limited and lofty states. "Produces the faculties" means that by making virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi) part of the states leading to penetration (nibbedha-bhāgiya), one produces the faculties such as faith (saddhā) which ripen liberation (vimutti). "When the faculties are being developed" means that when the aforementioned faculties are being increased, the full understanding (pariññā) of the known (ñeyya) occurs by way of comprehending materiality and mentality (rūpa-arūpa-pariggaha) and so on.

Full understanding as vision (dassana-pariññā) is full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). Full understanding as cultivation (bhāvanā-pariññā) consists of full understanding as investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) and full understanding as abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). The meaning stated briefly as "It is twofold" (sā duvidhā) and so on is expanded by "When indeed the trainee..." (yadā hi sekho) and so on. In that passage, by the words "with perceptions and attention associated with revulsion" (nibbidāsahagatehi saññāmanasikārehi), strong insight (balava-vipassanā) is shown. In the phrase "When indeed the trainee," a good worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) is also included under the term "trainee" (sekha) because of their habit of training; thus it is said: "Two states... reach skill, namely skill in vision..." and so on. The intention here is: when a good worldling, practicing the preliminary training, fully understands the known through perceptions and attention associated with revulsion, then those insight-states of his reach "skill in vision" (dassana-kosalla), which is the first path knowledge (paṭhamamagga-ñāṇa); they arrive at and connect with that path. But when a trainee such as a Stream-enterer fully understands the known in the manner stated, then those insight-states of his reach "skill in cultivation" (bhāvanā-kosalla).

"That knowledge" (taṃ ñāṇaṃ) refers to the full understanding of the known mentioned previously, meaning the knowledge that fully understands the known. By the phrase "should be known in five ways" (pañcavidhena veditabbaṃ), the diversity of that knowledge is shown according to the diversity of objects. "Knowledge of the individual characteristics of states" (dhammānaṃ salakkhaṇe ñāṇaṃ) is the knowledge that knows the individual characteristics of materiality and mentality, such as hardness (kakkhaḷa) and touching (phusana). Since all that is to be known is twofold as cause and effect, that knowledge is described as "analytical knowledge of states (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and analytical knowledge of meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā)."

In the term "full understanding" (pariññā), full understanding as investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) is intended. Because for that trainee, after specially knowing materiality and mentality by way of individual characteristics and causes, and after comprehending them through the divisions of wholesome and so on, the knowing by way of impermanence (anicca) and so on arises; therefore, it is said: "Having thus specially known, that full understanding which is 'this is wholesome'" and so on. In that passage, "thus comprehended" means comprehended and investigated by way of group-contemplation (kalāpa-sammasana) as impermanent and so on. "Produce this fruit" means they produce this fruit such as the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) in due order.
78:
They bring about (knowledge of rise and fall, etc.). Because the object which is the state to be investigated is metaphorically referred to by the role of the agent, it is said that (those states) bring about (the knowledge of rise and fall). It is just as the truths that make one an Ariya are called 'Ariya-saccas' (Noble Truths). 'Tesaṃ' refers to (the meaning of) the knowledge of rise and fall and so on. 'Evaṃgahitānaṃ' refers to those that are brought about (in such a way as impermanence, etc.). 'Ayaṃ attho' refers to the meaning of the appropriate understanding and the penetrative realization of the Truths. Just as the wisdom of full understanding (pariññā-paññā) fully understands the states to be investigated, the states that investigate, and the mode of investigation in those states to be investigated, so too it fully understands the fruit of investigation; thus, this method is shown.

By the phrase 'ye akusalā', the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) is spoken of. This is because all unwholesome states belong to the side of the Truth of the Origin. 'Ye kusalā' refers to the path-states (magga-dhamma) such as Right View and so on. Although it is true that the fruition-states (phala-dhamma) are also to be realized, because the penetration of the Four Truths is intended, it is said: "Which states are to be realized? The Unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) [is to be realized]." 'Attha-kusalo' means being skilled in the results produced by causes. 'Dhamma-kusalo' means being skilled in the causal states. Alternatively, the meaning of the Pali and the text of the Pali are called 'attha' and 'dhamma'. 'Kalyāṇatā-kusalo' means being skilled in suitability; the meaning is being expert in the four methods, or being skilled in the technique of teaching. 'Phalatā-kusalo' means being skilled in the fruition of Arahantship. In the words such as 'āya-kusalo', 'āya' means benefit (growth). That benefit is of two kinds: the non-loss of welfare and the arising of welfare. 'Apāya' means the absence of benefit. It is also of two kinds: the loss of welfare and the non-arising of welfare. 'Upāya' refers to the causal factor arising at that moment which is capable of remedying an urgent task or a danger that has arisen for beings; being skilled in that is the meaning. Because the Arahant (khīṇāsava) has abandoned ignorance (avijjā) in every way, he has reached the expansion of wisdom and is skilled in these areas such as benefit and so on. Having thus explained the skill of the Asekha (one beyond training) in part, the text says "He is endowed with great skill" to show it again without remainder.

For the Asekha who has completed the training, since there is no other purpose for acting with mindfulness, it is said: "For the sake of a pleasant dwelling in this very life." Now, wishing to conclude the practice of the Sekha and Asekha as described, the text says "These two practices," and so on. In that passage, 'bojjhaṃ' means that which is to be known. That which is to be known is of four kinds because of the nature of the Four Truths. One who knows by way of the full understanding of realization (pariññā-abhisamaya) and so on is called an 'Asekha'. That Asekha person who has reached the expansion of mindfulness is spoken of in the primary sense as "Being mindful, he proceeds," and so on. The remaining words have clear meanings. Here too, the selection of questions and answers should be understood according to the method previously mentioned.
79:
With this much extent of speech, while the Venerable Mahākaccāyana was analyzing the Mode of Investigation (vicaya-hāra), he showed the investigation of questions (pucchā-vicaya) and the investigation of answers (vissajjana-vicaya) by the power of the Ajita Sutta. Now, wishing to show the method of investigating questions and answers in other Suttas as well, he said: "Thus it should be asked, thus it should be answered." In that passage, "thus" means by this method. "Should be asked" means a question should be made, or should be told, or should be selected and investigated. In the phrase "thus it was answered," the method is the same. The words "suttassa ca" and so on are the demonstration of the investigation of the subsequent recitation (anugīti). The phrase "anugīti should be coordinated by way of meaning and by way of phrasing" means that the anugīti, known as the teaching of another Sutta, should be made similar to the Sutta being commented upon by way of meaning and phrasing, or it should be properly brought into coordination with that Sutta. "Atthāpagataṃ" means that which is devoid of meaning, or words with disconnected meanings like the phrase "ten pomegranates," etc. Therefore, he said: "It becomes frivolous talk (samphappalāpa)." By this, he states the reason for the necessity of coordinating the meaning. "Dunnikkhittassa" means of that which is badly expressed. "Dunnayo" means that which is to be understood with difficulty, or that which is impossible to lead [to understanding]. "Byañjanupetaṃ" means being endowed with natural terminology (nirutti).

Having thus shown the investigation of the subsequent recitation, in order to analyze the meaning stated briefly in the section of the exposition (niddesa-vāra) as "the investigation which is of the Sutta," he said "The Sutta also should be investigated," and wishing to show the manner of that investigation, he said: "Is this Sutta a direct discourse (āhacca-vacana)?" and so on. In that passage, "āhacca-vacana" means the speech produced by the Blessed One by striking the places of articulation; the meaning is the Sutta taught by the Fully Enlightened One himself. "Anusandhi-vacana" means that which is spoken by disciples. It should be known that such a disciple-spoken Sutta is called "anusandhi-vacana" because it proceeds by following the connection of the Blessed One's words. "Nītattha" refers to a Sutta whose meaning is to be understood according to the literal sound. "Neyyattha" refers to a Sutta whose meaning is to be taken by drawing it out. The meaning of terms such as "saṃkilesabhāgiya" (leading to defilement) will become clear in the explanation of the Paṭṭhāna-vāra. Since there is no teaching of the Blessed One that does not fall into one of the sixteen dispensational settings (sāsana-paṭṭhāna), that method is also placed here as something to be investigated.

"Where in this Sutta?" means in which part among the beginning, middle, and end of this Sutta. "All truths should be seen" means: in which part or in which word of the Sutta should the Truth of Suffering be seen, selected, and investigated? In which part should the Truth of the Origin, the Truth of Cessation, and the Truth of the Path be seen, observed, selected, and investigated? The intention is that all truths should be extracted and investigated in this way. "In the beginning, middle, and end" means that the Sutta should be investigated thus, from the beginning, from the middle...
80:
It means that the Sutta should be investigated in this way, through the method of investigating questions and so forth, at the beginning, middle, and end. In this Analysis of the Mode of Investigation (Vicaya-hāra-vibhaṅga), the investigation of questions (pucchā-vicaya), the investigation of answers (vissajjanā-vicaya), the investigation of what precedes and follows (pubbāpara-vicaya), and the investigation of subsequent recitation (anugīti-vicaya) are shown in the Pāḷi text by way of their own nature. However, the investigation of gratification and so forth (assādādivicaya) is shown by way of method, based on the disclosure of the Truths. That investigation of gratification and so forth should be understood according to the method stated in the Section of Exposition (Niddesavāra). Through such investigation, the investigation of words (padavicaya) is also accomplished.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Investigation is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Construing (Yutti-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā)

In that Analysis of the Mode of Construing, the passage beginning with "Tattha katamo yuttihāro" constitutes the Analysis of the Mode of Construing. In that Analysis, the question "What does it construe?" asks about the scope (visaya) of the Mode of Construing. What is the scope of this Mode of Construing? The meanings of the Sutta that are grasped in an incorrect manner are its scope. Those meanings of the Sutta grasped incorrectly must be construed by disclosing the logic (yutti) according to how they truly are, in an excellent manner, through this Mode of Construing. This Mode of Construing is desired in the other Modes (hāras) as well. However, such a desire is merely for the sake of stating the truth. Because this search for logic cannot exist without the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa), the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, while analyzing the Mode of Construing, spoke the words beginning with "Cattāro mahāpadesā" (The Four Great Authorities) to first point out the characteristics of that Mode of Construing.

Among those Great Authorities, 'mahāpadesa' means 'great references' (mahā-apadesa). It means great reasons stated by referring to great persons such as the Buddha. Alternatively, 'mahāpadesa' means 'great locations' (mahā-okāsa); it means the great standing-places of the Dhamma. In this context, the word-definition (vacanattha) is: it is called 'apadesa' because it is pointed out (apadiyyati). The Buddha is the person pointed out for this reason, thus it is called 'Buddha-apadesa'. This method applies to the remaining 'Saṅgha-apadesa' and so forth. It is the ground for deciding whether a text brought by someone saying, "I have heard this in the presence of the Blessed One," and so forth, is Dhamma or non-Dhamma. What is that ground? It is the 'entering into the Sutta' (suttotaraṇa) and so forth of the text thus brought. If so, why is it said to be four? It is fourfold by way of the distinction of the persons pointed out. There are two types of those who transmit (sampadāya) the Dhamma: the Blessed One and the disciples. Among them, the disciples are threefold by way of the Community (Saṅgha), the group (gaṇa), and the individual (puggala). There are four due to the distinction of the persons to be pointed out, as in "I received this Dhamma from such and such a person." Therefore, it is said, "Buddha-apadesa ... Ekatthera-apadesa." "Tāni padabyañjanāni" refers to the words and syllables of the Sutta brought by someone, meaning both the words of meaning (atthapada) and the words of phrasing (byañjanapada). Or, by way of the explanation of the commentator...
81:
The words and syllables that are brought "should be made to enter into the Sutta," which means they should be inserted into the Sutta. "Should be compared" means they should be correlated. "Should be placed against" means they should be included.

To show the Sutta and so forth, the passage beginning with "Katamasmiṃ" (In which?) was spoken. In showing those Suttas and so forth, because there is not even a single verse of the Blessed One's speech that is devoid of the Four Noble Truths, it is said, "In the Four Noble Truths," to show the meaning of the word "Sutta." In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), however, the Three Piṭakas are called "Sutta"; that statement of the Commentaries should be understood as being certainly correlated and in agreement with this Netti-pāḷi. As long as the Blessed One's teaching has the purpose of Final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna), that teaching certainly speaks of the subsiding of defilements such as lust. Therefore, wishing to show the meaning of the word "in the Vinaya," he said, "In the discipline of lust" and so forth. For here, "Vinaya" is intended as the cause for the subsiding of lust and so forth. As the Blessed One said:

"Gotamī, whatever qualities you may know: 'These qualities lead to passion, not to dispassion; they lead to bondage, not to release from bondage; they lead to the accumulation of rebirth, not to the dispersal of rebirth; they lead to great desires, not to fewness of desires; they lead to discontent, not to contentment; they lead to fondness for company, not to seclusion; they lead to laziness, not to the arousal of energy; they lead to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support'—Gotamī, you may definitely hold: 'This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher's instruction.' And Gotamī, whatever qualities you may know: 'These qualities lead to dispassion, not to passion; they lead to release from bondage, not to bondage; they lead to the dispersal of rebirth, not to the accumulation of rebirth; they lead to fewness of desires, not to great desires; they lead to contentment, not to discontent; they lead to seclusion, not to fondness for company; they lead to the arousal of energy, not to laziness; they lead to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support'—Gotamī, you may definitely hold: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction.'"

To show the meaning of the word "in the Nature of things" (dhammatāya), he said, "In Dependent Origination" (paṭiccasamuppāde). For Dependent Origination is stated as "that element which stands, the stability of the Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhitatā), the fixed course of the Dhamma (dhammaniyāmatā)."
82:
Although the phrase "Dhammatāyaṃ upanikkhipitabbāni" is not found in the Pāli Canon, it should be understood that it is stated here for the purpose of showing the meaning. In this context, when the arising (pavatti), cessation (nivatti), and the means for that arising and cessation are shown as being fixed in their nature of oppression and so forth, it is said to "descend into the Sutta" (otarati). When it is taught as the discipline of defilements such as lust (rāga) and so forth, it is said to "conform to the Vinaya" (sandissati). Likewise, when the nature of phenomena as causes and effects is clearly demonstrated by avoiding eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) and by showing the method of unity (ekatta-naya) and so forth, it is said "not to contradict the nature of things" (na vilometi).

Wishing to show this meaning—that such a collection of meanings and phrasing does not give rise to taints (āsava) such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava)—he said, "If in the four Noble Truths," and so forth. Dependent Origination in forward order is called arising (pavatti), and in reverse order, it is called cessation (nivatti). One might ask: since Dependent Origination is already included within the four Noble Truths, why is it taken separately here? That is true. However, the reason for taking it separately here is to show the nature of phenomena as being dependent on causes, thereby clarifying the characteristic of cause as impermanent, the characteristic of cause as incapable, and the characteristic of cause as effortless. It is also to show the connection with the three characteristics: their nature of having an arising, their nature of having a passing away because of that arising, their impermanence (aniccatā) due to both, and their suffering (dukkhatā) and non-self (anattatā) due to the oppression of arising and passing away. Furthermore, it is to make known the perfection of the Dispensation (sāsana-sampatti), which destroys all wrong views and evil thoughts and is not shared with others.

In this context, these four should be understood: the Sutta, the Great Authority in accordance with the Sutta (Suttānuloma), the Teachers' View (Ācariyavāda), and One's Own Opinion (Attanomati). Among these, "Sutta" refers to the Three Piṭakas as established in the three Councils. "Suttānuloma" refers to the Great Authorities called "Anulomakappiya." "Ācariyavāda" refers to the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). "Attanomati" refers to one's own intuition arising through the grasp of methods and subsequent understanding. Among these four, the Sutta is not to be rejected; one who rejects the Sutta rejects the Teacher himself. The Anulomakappiya should be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. The Teachers' View should also be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta, not otherwise. Likewise, One's Own Opinion should be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta. That "One's Own Opinion" is the weakest of all.

Now, to show the purpose for which the four Great Authorities are brought in here, he said, "By the four Great Authorities," and so forth. In that statement, "yaṃ yaṃ" refers to whatever meaning and whatever Pāli text. "Yujjati" means conforming to (not contradicting) the four Great Authorities mentioned. "Yena yena" means by whatever reason. "Yathā yathā" means in whatever manner. "Taṃ taṃ gahetabbaṃ" means by the reason and manner brought into the Sutta being explained, extracting from the Sutta by way of explanation...
83:
"Should be taken" is the meaning. Therefore, it is shown that one should determine the meanings from the Sutta by logic that does not contradict the four Great Authorities and apply the Yutti-hāra (Mode of Conveying Logic).

Now, to show that determination of logic, he began with "Pañhaṃ pucchitena," and so forth. In that statement, "kati padāni" means how many words. To show the meaning of the word "pariyogāhitabbaṃ," it is said "vicetabbaṃ" (should be investigated). As many words as express the intended meaning, those words are called "one question" because of the desire to know that single meaning. Whether all the words in a verse or just a single word expresses a single meaning, that is just one question; this meaning is shown by "yadi sabbāni," and so forth. "Taṃ" refers to that question. "Aññātabbaṃ" means should be known. "Kiṃ ime dhammā," and so forth, shows the manner of knowing. In that context, "dhammā" refers to the scriptural teachings (pariyatti-dhamma). "Nānatthā" means do they have different meanings?

In the question verse, the word-meaning is as follows: "Kenassubbhāhato loko" means by what is this world of beings struck and killed, like a thief by an executioner? "Kenassu parivါrito" means by what is the world enveloped, like a māluva creeper covering a tree? "Kena sallena otiṇṇo" means by what kind of dart is it pierced, like a poison-tipped arrow sinking into the body? "Kissa dhūpāyito" means for what reason is the world heated and fuming? The word "sadā" (always) should be applied to all the phrases. "Te" refers to the four words. Because it regards the word "pañha" (question), it is indicated in the masculine gender. By the word "vissajjeti" (he answers), it is shown that there are three questions because of the answering.

In that context, in the answer verse, old age (jarā) mentioned in the second line and death (maraṇa) mentioned in the first line are the characteristics of the conditioned (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa) because the five conditioned aggregates are marked as "conditioned" by these. For the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these three characteristics of the conditioned. Which three? Arising (uppāda) is manifest, passing away (vaya) is manifest, and the alteration of what is present (ṭhitassa aññathatta) is manifest." Therefore, it is said: "Old age is the alteration of what is present, and death is the passing away." Here, by the phrase "alteration of what is present," it is shown that "old age" here refers to the difference between the earlier and later stages of the continuity of aggregates, not the momentary presence (khaṇa-ṭṭhiti). By the phrase "death is the passing away," it also refers to conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa) as commonly spoken of in the world, such as "Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead." It does not refer to momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa) or death as final cutting off (samuccheda-maraṇa).

Now, to show the meaning stated as "those three questions" by the power of logic, he began with "Jarāya cā," and so forth. In showing it by logic, since one usually sees only the death of the aged, for those who do not wish to admit the distinction between old age and death, he said "Gacchagatāpi hi mီyanti" (for even the young die) to show the distinction between old age and death.
84:
"Phussa is dead"—this refers to conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa) as spoken of in the world; it does not refer to momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa) or death by extirpation (samuccheda-maraṇa).

Now, to demonstrate the meaning of "those three questions" through logic, the phrase beginning with "Jarāya ca" is stated. In this logical demonstration, because death is mostly seen in the aged, to show the distinction between aging (jarā) and death (maraṇa) to those who do not accept it, it is said: "Even those in the womb die." The meaning is this: since death is seen without the intended aging, aging is one thing and death is another. Therefore, it is said: "They are not aged."

Furthermore, just as pure death is seen unmixed with the aging of devas, because pure death is seen, aging is one thing and death is another; this meaning is shown by the phrase beginning with "It exists for devas too." Aging can be counteracted by treatment with superior human qualities (such as jhāna), but death cannot be treated in that way. To show that the distinction in meaning between aging and death should be accepted for this reason, the phrase beginning with "Sakkateva" is stated. In that context, "sakkate" means it is possible or capable. "Paṭikammaṃ" means counteraction or remedy.

Considering the objection, "If there is mastery in the development of the bases of power (iddhipāda), can death not also be counteracted?" he said: "Except for the sphere of power of the powerful ones." The Blessed One said this:
"Ānanda, whoever has developed, practiced, made a vehicle of, made a basis of, established, consolidated, and well-undertaken the four bases of power, if he so desires, he could remain for an aeon (kappa) or for the remainder of an aeon."

What is an aeon here, and what is the remainder of an aeon? An aeon means a lifespan (āyukappa). Whatever the lifespan of humans is at a particular time, one who completes that lifespan is said to remain for an aeon. One who remains beyond the hundred-year lifespan, etc., as stated by "a little more," is said to remain for the remainder of an aeon.

If they can remain so, why do the Arahants, who possess great power and mastery over the mind, not remain for the benefit of the world? It is because they have fully understood the burden of suffering known as the aggregates (khandha) and because they have no desire to strive [to remain]. Indeed, those superior persons have stilled all striving. The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, said this:
"I do not delight in death, nor do I desire life. I only await the time [of Parinibbāna], as a laborer awaits his wages."
85:
Just as aging and death are distinct from each other in meaning, so too when the distinction between aging-and-death and craving (taṇhā) is shown, the statement "three questions" (tayo pañhā) is accomplished. To show this, the phrase beginning with "Yaṃ pana" is stated.

In that context, because aging and death are found in the continuity of Arahants even in the absence of craving, the meaning that aging-and-death is one thing and craving is another is stated by the passage: "Those free from passion are seen both aging and dying." If it is asked, "Does craving not also have the nature of aging and breaking up?"—it is true, but the meaning intended here is that this aging and death is not that momentary aging and death. By the phrase beginning with "Yadi ca," the fault that would arise if aging-and-death and craving were not different (i.e., were the same) is shown. The meaning is that even those in their youth would be free from craving, which is not appropriate.

If aging-and-death and craving were not different, aging-and-death would also be the origin (samudaya) of suffering. If they were not different, craving would also not be the origin of suffering. In reality, aging-and-death is not the origin of suffering; only craving is the origin of suffering. Therefore, it should be understood that these are distinct in meaning. Just as craving is to be abandoned by the Path (magga), if it were not different from craving, aging-and-death would also have to be abandoned by the Path. Just as aging-and-death is not abandoned by the Path, craving would also not be abandoned by the Path. This method should also be noted as previously stated. "Imāya yuktiyā" means by the aforementioned reason. "Aññamaññehi" means if the distinction in meaning is clear through other reasons, the distinction should also be sought through the phrasing (byañjana).

The identity in meaning of these factors is explained by the phrase beginning with "Na hi yujjati." By the phrase "when the desire of craving is not fulfilled," it refers to not obtaining what is desired. Thus, it amounts to saying that wish (icchā) and craving (taṇhā) are identical in meaning. Just as this statement is valid in that wish and craving are not distinct in meaning, so too is the statement valid that when there is the opposite of wish (unfulfillment), anger (kodha) and malice (upanāha) arise in the grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu). This is not the case with the opposite of aging-and-death. Therefore, the distinction in meaning between aging-and-death and craving is established by the phrase beginning with "Imāya yuktiyā."

If wish and craving are identical in meaning, why did the Blessed One state them as two in this verse? The resolution to that objection is stated by the phrase beginning with "Yaṃ panidaṃ." There, "yaṃ" is a term referring to the action. "Abhilapitaṃ" means "stated" (vuttaṃ).
86:
Expression (abhilapana) should be understood as being connected to external objects such as forms, either by way of the object itself or by way of making it an object. 'By two things' means by two natures. What are those two natures? Icchā (desire) is the seeking of an object not yet obtained. Taṇhā (craving) is the desire to consume an object, whether obtained or not yet obtained. This is the distinction between them. Even though there is such a distinction, to show that all craving is of one nature by way of swallowing and completely seizing objects such as forms, it is said: 'All craving has but one characteristic, the characteristic of clinging (ajjhosāna).'

Now, to clarify this meaning with a simile, it is said: 'All fire...', which is easy to understand. This craving is not only spoken of by two names according to its mode of occurrence regarding the object, but also by many other synonyms; to show this, it is said: 'as icchā also,' and so on.

Therein, it is called icchā because one desires objects through it. It is called taṇhā in the sense of lusting. It is called salla (dart) because it causes affliction and is difficult to extract, like a poisoned dart. It is called dhūpāyanā (fuming) in the sense of causing burning. It is called saritā (river) because it pulls like a river with a swift current, or saritā in the sense of being moist. For it is said: 'To beings there arise joys that are moistened by affection and attached by joy' (Dhammapada 341). 'Moistened and attached' is the meaning here.

Visattikā is so called because it spreads (visata). (Visata is also called visaṭa). It is called visattikā because it is uneven (visama). It is called visattikā because it is vast (visāla). It is called visattikā because it vibrates or struggles (visakkati). It is called visattikā because it causes failure (visamvādikā). It is called visattikā because it confuses the mind (or brings suffering - visamharati). It is called visattikā because it has suffering as its root (visamūlā). It is called visattikā because it has suffering as its fruit (visaphala). It is called visattikā because it consumes only suffering (visaparibhoga). Or else, that craving is called visattikā because it is spread and expanded (visata vitthata) among forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, mental objects, families, and groups.

It is called sineha (affection) by way of being moist. It is called kilamatha (fatigue) because it causes weariness in various destinations (gati). It is called latā (creeper) in the sense of entwining. For it is said: 'The creeper (craving) arises and stands' (Dhammapada 340). It is called maññanā (imagining) by way of thinking 'mine'. It is called bandha (bond) in the sense of pulling and binding even what is far away. It is called āsā (expectation) in the sense of desiring. It is called pipāsā (thirst) by way of wanting to drink the flavor of the object. It is called abhinandanā (delighting) in the sense of greatly rejoicing. Thus, although it is grasped by many names according to its mode of occurrence regarding the object, all craving has but one characteristic, the characteristic of clinging (ajjhosāna); thus the aforementioned meaning is concluded.
87:
Furthermore, the fact that craving is grasped by many names is shown with the word 'ca' (and) which has a cumulative sense, as in 'And as...', and so on. Regarding the term vevacana (synonym), I shall explain the meaning of the verse 'Expectation and thirst' (āsā ca pipāsā) in the Vevacana-hāra-vibhaṅga itself. In the passages such as 'of one whose lust is not gone' (avigatarāgassa), craving itself is meant by rāga in the sense of lusting, chanda in the sense of desiring, pema in the sense of affection, and paridāha in the sense of burning. Therefore, it is said: 'This is a synonym (vevacana) for craving.' In this way, since icchā and taṇhā are not different in meaning, the statement 'three questions' is appropriate and consistent with logic.

Having thus shown the logic for the 'three questions' in the verse 'By what is the world led away?' (Kenassubbhāhato loko), he now says 'All occurrence of suffering' (sabbo dukkhūpacāro), etc., to show the search for logic through other methods. Therein, dukkhūpacāra means the occurrence of suffering. Kāmatanhā-saṅkhāra-mūlaka means having the cause of formations (saṅkhāra) which have sensual craving as their support; this is intended to be appropriate. Nibbidūpacāra means the occurrence of disenchantment (nibbidā). Discontent (anabhirati) arising from the change and alteration of sensual pleasures, and knowledge-based disenchantment (ñāṇa-nibbidā), are called nibbidūpacāra. Kāmatanhā-parikkhāra-mūlaka means having as its cause the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma) which are the requisites of sensual craving. Between those two, only the disenchantment known as discontent has the objects of sensuality as its cause; knowledge-based disenchantment does not have the requisites of sensual craving as its cause. Therefore, the statement 'All occurrence of disenchantment is rooted in the requisites of sensual craving' is intended to be inappropriate. With the phrase 'By this logic' (imāya yuttiyā), he shows the method of searching for logic. This is what is meant: Just as logic was stated for the three questions, and for the occurrence of suffering and disenchantment, so too, by this logic and by this method, logic should be sought in various Pali passages through other appropriate causes.

Now, as the showing of that method is very brief, he begins 'For as the Blessed One...' (yathā hi bhagavā), etc., to analyze and show it in detail. Here is the summary of the meaning: For persons of lustful, hateful, and deluded temperaments, the teaching of foulness (asubha), loving-kindness (mettā), and the discourse on dependent origination (paccaya-ākāra-kathā) in due order is suitable because it removes lust and so on. This is the logic of the Dispensation (sāsana-yutti). While it stands in this suitable way, if one were to teach the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti) to one of lustful temperament, that teaching would not be appropriate because it is unsuitable. Likewise, 'pleasant progress' (sukhā-paṭipadā), etc., (if taught to one of lustful temperament) are inappropriate. One might object: 'Do not pleasant progress and so on occur only in practice (paṭipatti), and not in teaching (desanā)?' This is true. However, here, 'one of lustful temperament' means one with sharp defilements. For such a person, meditation is accomplished through painful progress (dukkhā-paṭipadā). For one whose meditation is accomplished through painful progress, the very heavy teaching on foulness is suitable. For one for whom the very heavy teaching on foulness is suitable, a heavy teaching is not inappropriate. To show this meaning, he said: 'Whether pleasant... teaching'.
88:
Meditation is fulfilled. For one for whom meditation is fulfilled through painful practice, the very heavy teaching on foulness is suitable. For one for whom the very heavy teaching on foulness is suitable, it is not the case that a very light teaching is suitable, as it would be for one with weak defilements. To show this meaning, it is said: "Whether a pleasant practice... etc... the teaching would be preached, it is not fitting." In this way, the meaning should be stated for the remaining terms as they occur. In this Yutti-hāra, since the acquisition of correct logic is through the rejection of what is unfitting, one should also search for what is unfitting when considering logic; thus it is said: "If indeed... etc... the teaching is not fitting." The same method applies to the remaining cases. Thus, "Whatever..." and so forth is merely showing the method in applying the Yutti-hāra.

Therein, "thus" (evaṃ) means by this method. "Whatever" (yaṃ kiñci) means any other nature. "Conformable abandonment" (anulomappahānaṃ) means suitable for abandonment, capable of abandoning. The investigation of the meanings of the terms in the sutta without remainder, according to the sequence of terms, is called Vicaya-hāra. Because it is easy to search for logic in the meanings determined by the explanation of Vicaya-hāra, it is said: "Having investigated all that with the Vicaya-hāra, it should be applied with the Yutti-hāra." "As far as the ground of knowledge" (yāvatikā ñāṇassa bhūmi) means whatever knowledge and whatever intuition (paṭibhāna) the explaining teacher has, whatever the scope (visaya) of that knowledge is, that much is the procedure of the Yutti-hāra. Why is that? Because the True Dhamma has infinite methods, is beautiful in every way, can withstand scrutiny, and consists of diverse teachings.

Since the application of the Yutti-hāra has been shown only by way of demonstrating the method, the beginning "For one who abides in loving-kindness, being mindful..." is started to show it by classifying it through the Brahmavihāra, the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), and the mastery (vasībhāva) of the nine successive attainments. Therein, "for one who abides in loving-kindness" (mettāvihārissa) means for one who has attained the abiding in loving-kindness. "Mindful" (sato) means being so, for one who is such. "Ill-will" (byāpāda) is the resentment that destroys the mind. "It will stand having overwhelmed the mind" (cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati) means it will oppress the mind. Since there is no such thing as the simultaneous occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states, the word "will stand" (ṭhassati) is used to show that it will overwhelm and remain in the mind at a later time after emerging from the attainment. "The teaching is not fitting" (na yujjati desanā) means that because loving-kindness is the opposite of ill-will, such a statement is not fitting. The teaching "Ill-will goes to abandonment and destruction" is fitting; this means that for the reason already stated, this statement is fitting. In the remaining sections (vāra) also, the meaning should be understood in this very way. I shall explain only the obscure terms.

"For one who abides in the signless" (animittavihārissa) means for one who abides in the attainment of fruition obtained through the gateway of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). "Follower of signs" (nimittānusārī) means one who follows the signs of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta). That very...
89:
Among the signs of permanence and so forth, whichever sign has been abandoned, one is free by that very sign. "The 'I am' is gone" (asmīti vigataṃ) means that whatever thinking "I am" existed through the power of view and conceit regarding the five aggregates of clinging, that thinking has disappeared. He explains that very meaning with the text: "I do not regard this as 'I am'." In the phrase "the barb of doubt and indecision" (vicikicchā-kathaṃkathā-sallaṃ), even the remorse regarding discipline (vinaya-kukkucca) is specifically shown by the term "doubt" (vicikicchā) because it has the nature of occurring as "how is it?". "The teaching is not fitting" (na yujjati desanā) means that because doubt and [wrong] view have the same basis in being abandoned, this statement is not fitting. "For one who has attained the first jhāna" (paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa) means for one possessed of the first jhāna. The statement "Lust and ill-will lead to the distinction of the second jhāna" is not fitting. The reason is that if the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are not yet abandoned, even the access concentration (upacāra) of the first jhāna cannot occur, let alone the jhāna itself; therefore, the statement that lust and ill-will lead to the distinction of the second jhāna is not fitting. However, the teaching that lust and ill-will, having reached the stage of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), lead to the decline of the already obtained first jhāna is a fitting statement. In this way, it should be applied and understood in all cases. The perceptions and mental applications accompanied by the absence of initial thought (avitakka-sahagatā saññā-manasikārā) are the states of the second jhāna together with its access. Here, the word "accompanied" (sahagata) has the meaning of taking as an object. "For decline" (hānāya) means for falling away from the first jhāna. "For distinction" (visesāya) means for the sake of the second jhāna. By this method, the states mentioned as "decline" (hāna) and "distinction" (visesa) in various sections should be understood. "Accompanied by initial and sustained thought" (vitakka-vicāra-sahagatā) are the states of the first jhāna, or they are simply states of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). "Accompanied by equanimity and pleasure" (upekkhā-sukha-sahagatā) are the states of the second jhāna together with its access; here, "equanimity" (upekkhā) refers to specific neutrality (tatramajjhattūpekkhā). "Accompanied by rapture and pleasure" (pīti-sukha-sahagatā) are the states of the third jhāna together with its access. "Accompanied by the purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi-sahagatā) are the states of the fourth jhāna.

"Access to perception" (saññūpacāra) refers to any mental arisings (cittuppāda) that perform the function of clear perception; some also call them "states of the base of nothingness" (ākiñcaññāyatana-dhamma). "Accompanied by the cessation of perception and feeling" (saññāvedayitanirodha-sahagatā) refers to the states occurring by way of the preliminary work (parikamma) for that cessation, thinking "I shall abide having reached the cessation of perception and feeling." However, since only one who stands in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception can abide having reached the cessation of perception and feeling, and not one who has fallen away from it, the statement that they lead to the decline of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not fitting. But the statement that they lead to distinction (the attainment of cessation) is fitting; intending this, he said: "For decline... etc... the teaching." "Cultivated by proficiency" (kallatā-paricitaṃ) means cultivated by way of capability, meaning cultivated by way of mastery (vasībhāva) in the aforementioned attainments. Therefore, he said: "It is fit for directing [the mind] (abhinīhāraṃ khamati)." All the rest is clear.
90: Alternatively, in this Yutti-hāra, the saying 'By way of the perception of the non-repulsive (appaṭikkūlasaññā), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of the perception of the repulsive (paṭikkūlasaññā), ill will (byāpāda) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of concentration (samādhi), sloth and torpor (thinamiddha) deceive' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of the arousal of energy (vīriyārambha), restlessness (uddhacca) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of the desire for training (sikkhākāmatā), remorse (kukkucca) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of the investigation of both sides (ubhayapakkhasantīraṇa), doubt (vicikicchā) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of equanimity towards the desirable and undesirable (iṭṭhāniṭṭhasamupekkhaṇa), delusion (sammoha) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of knowing oneself (attaññutā), conceit (māna) in the form of not despising oneself deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of investigation (vīmaṃsā), wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) deceives through the wrong grasping of what resembles a cause' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of being dispassionate, lack of compassion towards beings deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of indulging in what is allowable, devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi), the habit of not sharing deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of the habit of sharing, wrong livelihood (micchājīva) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of living without socializing, the habit of not being helpful deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of the habit of being helpful, improper socializing deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of speaking the truth, slanderous speech (pisuṇavācā) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of not slandering, the lack of desire for welfare deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of speaking endearing words, flattery (cāṭukamyatā) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of speaking moderately, the habit of not speaking pleasantly deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of the habit of speaking pleasantly, deceit (māyā) and hypocrisy (sāṭheyya) deceive' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of speaking to reprove, harsh speech (pharusavācā) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of blaming evil, the habit of looking for others' faults deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of compassion for one's family, stinginess regarding families (kulamacchariya) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of the desire for the long-lastingness of the monastery, stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsamacchariya) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of removing obstacles to the Dhamma, stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhammamacchariya) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of delighting in preaching the Dhamma, delight in talk (bhassārāmatā) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of having non-harsh speech and supporting the group, delight in company (saṅgaṇikārāmatā) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of desiring merit, delight in work (kammārāmatā) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), mental distress deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of being full of faith, lack of investigation deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of investigation, lack of faith (assaddhiya) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of making oneself the authority, the failure to respectfully accept the instructions of teachers deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of making the Dhamma the authority, lack of respect for fellow practitioners deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of making the world the authority, the despising of oneself and the Dhamma deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'By way of the cultivation of loving-kindness, lust (rāga) deceives' is appropriate. The saying 'Under the guise of compassion (karuṇā), sorrow (soka) deceives' is appropriate. Under the guise of dwelling in appreciative joy (muditā)...
91:
It is fitting to say that joy (pahāsa) deceives. It is fitting to say that the relinquishing of desire for wholesome states under the guise of dwelling in equanimity (upekkhā-vihāra) deceives. In this way, the deceptive nature of those various states such as the guise of scripture (āgama) and the guise of attainment (adhigama) should be understood through logic. Thus, the search for logic should be conducted based on the sequence of scripture.

## The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Logic is finished.

## 4. Padatthāna-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā (The Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes)

In that (Netti-pāḷi), the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes is presented, beginning with "What is the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes?" In that Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes, the mode which has the characteristic of clarifying the states that are the proximate causes of various other states, such as "this state is the proximate cause (padatthāna) of that state; this state is the proximate cause of that state," is called the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes (Padatthāna-hāra). Therefore, starting with ignorance (avijjā), which is the root of the round of suffering, and wishing to extract and show the proximate cause of natural phenomena, the Buddha described the nature of ignorance: "Ignorance is characterized by the non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena."

The meaning of that statement is: through this ignorance, the undistorted nature of all phenomena is not penetrated; therefore, it is called "non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena" (sabbadhamma-yāthāva-asampativedha). Since such non-penetration is the characteristic of this ignorance, it is described as such. By this, it is meant that ignorance is the state characterized by the concealment of the nature of phenomena. Alternatively, right penetration is called penetration (sampativedha). Its opposite is non-penetration (asampativedha). As to where that opposite of penetration occurs, he said: "characterized by... all [phenomena]." Because when there is perversion (vipallāsa) such as [perceiving] the beautiful in the foul (asubha), delusion (sammoha) regarding those states only arises further and further and does not diminish; therefore, it is said: "That perversion is the proximate cause of ignorance."

"Piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ" means that states of a lovable and agreeable nature are the proximate cause. For has it not been taught: "Whatever in the world is of a lovable nature and an agreeable nature, there this craving, when arising, arises"? "Adinnādāna" means the intention of taking what is not given. Even if that intention arises only once, because of the failure to see the danger, it becomes the cause for the arising of greed; therefore, it is called the proximate cause of greed. The proximate cause of hatred is the taking of life (pāṇātipāta), and the proximate cause of delusion is wrong practice (micchā-patipadā); in these cases too, the meaning should be understood in this same manner. "Characterized by the grasping of color, shape, and features" means characterized by the grasping of signs (nimitta) and secondary features (anubyañjana). The characteristic of approaching contact (phassa) through the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā) is stated as having contact as its condition. For has it not been taught: "Being touched, one perceives"?
92:
Gratification (assāda) means craving (taṇhā). The characteristics of the conditioned (sankhata-lakkhaṇa) are arising, vanishing, and alteration. Generally, because the grasping of permanence is dependent on consciousness, it is said that consciousness (viññāṇa) is the proximate cause of the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā). This is because that monk, thinking 'this very consciousness runs and wanders from birth to birth,' expressed his own grasping of permanence by taking consciousness as the object. If impermanence (anicca) and suffering (dukkha) are clearly seen in the five aggregates, there is no more opportunity for the perception of self (atta-saññā) and the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā). Therefore, he said: "The characteristic of not closely contemplating the perception of impermanence and the perception of suffering is the perception of self." For has it not been taught: "What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self"?

Since the obsession with self generally occurs regarding mental phenomena, he said: "The mental body (nāma-kāya) is the proximate cause of that perception of self." "All that is knowable" (sabbaṃ neyyaṃ) refers to the Four Noble Truths, because there is no knowable thing outside of the Four Noble Truths. The removal of mental distraction is the suppression of restlessness (uddhacca). "Asubha" refers to the contemplation of foulness (asubha-anupassanā) or the foul objects themselves which become the counterpart sign (patibhāga-nimitta). Because it is the opposite of craving, it is said that foulness is the proximate cause of tranquility (samatha). Because it attenuates greed, abstaining from taking what is not given is said to be the proximate cause of non-greed (alobha). Likewise, because it attenuates ill-will, abstaining from taking life is said to be the proximate cause of non-hatred (adosa). "Vatthu-avippatipatti" (non-deviation from the object) is the penetration of the nature of the object. Right practice (sammā-patipadā) is the fulfillment of virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi). The knowledge of non-delight (anabhirati-ñāṇa) through the knowledge of disenchantment is itself the disenchantment (nibbida) that arises in that way. Because all feelings are suffering by way of the suffering of suffering (dukkha-dukkhatā) and so on, it is said: "Feeling (vedanā) is the proximate cause of the perception of suffering."

Since the lack of fading away of lust for the bodies of beings occurs by way of the five internal bases, he said: "The five material faculties are the proximate cause of lust for form (rūpa-rāga)." Here, "body" (kāya) is intended as form (rūpa). Since attachment occurs especially in the mind-base (manāyatana), which is the support for jhāna, he said: "The sixth base (chattāyatana) is the proximate cause of lust for existence (bhava-rāga)." The delight in form and so on that arises as "May such form not arise, may such feeling not arise" is called the contemplation of arisen existence (nibbatta-bhavānupassitā). "Knowledge and vision" (ñāṇa-dassana) means the knowledge and vision of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā). For one who has wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra), the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati) is the cause for the knowledge of the ownership of kamma; it is not so for one who emerges [from the round] without wise attention. To clarify this meaning, the Mahānārada-kassapa Jātaka and the partial eternalism (ekacca-sassata-vāda) in the Brahmajāla Sutta should be cited as examples. By the words "characterized by conviction (okappana)," etc., he shows the distinction between faith (saddhā) and confidence (pasāda). That confidence should be understood as a specific state of faith itself. There, conviction (okappana) is the plunging into and the decision upon the object by way of believing.
93:
The state of the mind being unclouded due to the absence of lack of faith is called non-turbidity (anāvilatā). Aspiration (abhipatthanā) is simply faith itself. The great clarity of mind accompanied by wisdom, having the Triple Gem as its object, is called confirmed confidence (aveccappasāda). Non-forgetfulness is called non-drifting (apilāpana); or, it is the entering into an object as if diving into it. Regarding the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of faith and so on, it should be understood that the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, in stating that clarity, faith, right effort, foundations of mindfulness, and factors of absorption are proximate causes in due order, spoke of their being proximate causes by way of specific stages. Alternatively, by way of being the proximate cause of mindfulness and concentration, the physical body and so on are called foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and initial thought and so on are called factors of absorption (jhānaṅga).

Contemplation of gratification in things that are objects of the fetters is called attention to gratification (assādamanasikāra). Germination of renewed existence (punabbhavavirohaṇā) means the sprouting of renewed existence, the state of being fit for arising in a new existence, and the nature of producing results. The characteristic of arising through rebirth (opapaccayikanibbattilakkhaṇā) means the nature of arising by way of the existence of rebirth. The characteristic of the combination of the mental body and the physical body (nāmakāyarūpakāyasaṅghātalakkhaṇā) means the nature of the grouping of the mental and physical bodies. The state of the six faculties, such as the eye, being determined is called determination of the faculties (indriyavavatthāna). Arising through rebirth (opapaccayika) means that which causes the aggregates of rebirth to arise. Substratum (upadhi) is the individual personality (attabhāva). Since sorrow (soka) usually arises in a fool who contemplates the death of a loved one, death (maraṇa) is said to be the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of sorrow. Anxiety (ussukka) is the burning of the mind. Burning (odahana) means intense burning (avadahana); it is the burning of one's own support. To show existence (bhava), the phrase 'these [factors of existence]' and so on is stated. Therein, both the causes of existence and the parts called existence are factors of existence (bhavaṅgāni). Among these two, defilements are the causes (factors) of existence. The round of kamma and the round of results are the parts (factors) called existence. Complete (samaggāni) means all. The wandering on (saṃsāra) is the successive arising of the aggregates, sense bases, and so on. Since the round of defilements and so on, produced in previous births, is the cause of that wandering on, it is said: 'Existence is the proximate cause of saṃsāra'. With reference to being the cause that leads [to Nibbāna], it is said: 'The path is the proximate cause of cessation (nirodha)'.

A person of great learning is called a 'ford' (tittha) because they are the landing place for a practitioner entering the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Proper attendance upon such a person of great learning is 'knowing the ford' (titthaññutā). Joy connected with the Dhamma is called 'pīta'. Producing that joy by listening to the suitable Dhamma and thereby increasing the meditation subject is 'knowing joy' (pītaññutā). Knowing the occurrence of even a slight degree of sluggishness (laya) or agitation (uddhacca) in meditation is 'knowing attainment' (pattanyutā). Knowing oneself as being endowed with the five factors of striving is 'knowing oneself' (attanyutā). Among these factors, it is easily understood that each preceding factor is the proximate cause of each succeeding one. Living in a suitable locality is possible only for one who has performed merit.
94:
Living in a suitable locality is possible for one who has performed merit, but not for another. Therefore, it is said: 'The state of having performed merit in the past is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of living in a suitable locality'. Tender insight together with the knowledge of the known (ñātapariññā), which is the basis for the knowledge of investigation (tīraṇapariññā), is called 'knowledge and vision of things as they are' (yathābhūtañāṇadassana). Disenchantment (nibbidā) is strong insight. Fading of lust (virāga) is the path. Liberation (vimutti) is the fruit.

Thus, the proximate cause of ignorance and so on has been shown by such statements as 'The perversion (vipallāsa) of that [ignorance] is its proximate cause'. By this method, it should be understood that any strong dependence (upanissaya) or any other remaining condition—all such causes are proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna). They also read: 'Thus, whatever the cause (upanisā) may be, by way of logic and by way of condition'. Therein, 'cause' (upanisā) means the reason; 'by way of logic' (yogato) means by way of reasoning; 'by way of condition' (paccayato) means simply by way of being a condition. This is how the meaning should be understood. What has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning in this Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Proximate Cause is easily understood.

## The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Proximate Cause is finished.

## 5. Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇa-hāra-vibhaṅga)

Therein, the section beginning with 'Which is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics?' is the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics. Therein, by the question 'What is characterized?', the scope (visaya) of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics is asked. Having shown the Mode of Conveying Characteristics briefly with the words 'Those things which...', the section beginning with 'eye' (cakkhu) is commenced to analyze it with examples (udāharaṇa). Therein, by the statement 'they have a single characteristic in the sense of a murderer', it should be understood that the state of having a single characteristic is also stated by way of impermanence (anicca) and so on.

Having thus shown the state of having a single characteristic by way of the sense bases (āyatana), the Sutta beginning with 'Rādha, one should be without desire for the past form' is cited to show it now by way of the aggregates and so on. In the Yamakovāda Sutta (SN 3.85), it is stated that they have a single characteristic in the sense of a murderer. It is so stated because it appears in that Sutta as 'He does not understand as it really is: form is a murderer, form is a murderer', and so on. Thus, in this verse, when mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) is mentioned, it means that mindfulness directed to feelings, mindfulness directed to the mind, and mindfulness directed to mental phenomena are also mentioned, because they have a single characteristic by way of being foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). The meaning of terms such as 'seen' (diṭṭha) and others will be explained later.
95:
In the text “Kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi,” “kāye” refers to the physical body (rūpa-kāya). Indeed, in this Dispensation, the physical body is intended as “kāya” in the sense of a collection (samūha) of major and minor limbs, hair, and so on. Just as it is intended as “kāya” in the sense of a collection, it is also intended as “kāya” in the sense of being the place of origin (āya) of loathsome (kucchita) things such as hair and so on.
